Mr. Chairman, several sound reasons have been advanced in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) and seconded by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). These reasons have been elaborated, and I do not propose to go over the same ground, but I do wish to register my support of the principle of the amendment, namely, that we extend the charters of the banks for one year, thus allowing further time for the consideration of the mass of evidence taken before the Banking committee. To my mind the Banking committee have done excellent work in the taking of evidence. There is a large amount of material available for the consideration of the members of the House, but unless the members have ample time to give it their considered judgment I feel that the evidence will not reach its full value to us as a parliament. Probably a great many of the members of that committee feel that they have had time to consider the evidence, but I know that a number of them do not; much less have the members of this House who were not on that committee had time to consider it. The Minister of Finance has said that the evidence has been before the country in the publications of the committee and in the press, but I do not feel that the country has had sufficient time to give it the consideration that is required. A number of letters have been received by many members of this House urging that the consideration of this act be postponed for another year. The hon. member for Red Deer has referred to the requests of the Alberta and Manitoba governments for postponement of consideration, and I think that these requests should carry considerable weight. Organized agriculture through the Canadian Council of Agriculture has also asked for a postponement of consideration, and I believe that organized labour is also of the same opinion. I think, Sir, that this weight of opinion should not be passed over lightly.
We are not in this amendment asking for anything for which there is not a precedent. I believe the same course was followed in May, 1911, and also in April, 1912. I feel that there is no sound reason why we should hurry this thing through unduly. I do not see why there is such a terrific rush to consider this act and get it out of the way. The banking system of this country is one of the most vital questions that we have to consider and I cannot help feeling that we should have further time to consider the evidence. I cannot see how any public interest will be prejudiced by a postponement of consideration of the act. I do not think that the banks themselves have anything to fear from that. We are men of reasonable judgment I think in this House, and I believe that the public interest will best be served by a postponement of consideration of the act for one year. For this reason and for the reasons that have been given by the hon. member for Red Deer I propose to support the amendment.

In rising to support the amendment which has been moved I desire to make a few comments on the continuation of our banking system as we now have it. I think all members will agree that conditions at the present time are very unstable. There is a good deal of dissatisfaction throughout the country at large and I think it would be a very unpopular thing to renew these bank charters as we now have them. It would almost be a proclamation that we had decided that our banking system was as good as we could hope to make it, or that we had decided that we would not go to the trouble of studying it and investigating other systems which have been proposed.
May I also call attention to the fact that at the present time marketing conditions from a world standpoint are almost an impossibility. We find many countries that are badly in need of the produce we are able to grow in Canada, but we find that their currency is so depreciated that they are unable to buy our produce. On the other hand, our banks are making a very strenuous effort to get back to the gold standard. I do not think that anything could be done that would so much retard the development of Canada as that, for if we get back to the gold standard and some of the countries to which we hope to sell have a greatly depreciated currency it would mean that those countries already debt-ridden would have to pay three and four times the ordinary price to buy what we have to sell, and we would have to take less. It is
Bank Act

an impossible position, and I do not think it can be continued.
There have been placed before the Banking committee three different proposals for a banking system which might give better satisfaction than the one we have at the present time. I venture to say that there is not a member of this House or a member of the Banking and Commerce committee who fully understands any one of those three systems, and surely there could be no objection to renewing these charters for another year in order to give us time to study these systems and find out if there is not a possibility at least of adapting one of them to our needs.
I would also add that in practically every country there are students at present studying the financial problem. Now if we renew our bank charters I should think it would discourage those students who are making a study of the banking system of Canada. I would almost think that they would interpret it in one of two ways: They would either say that we have a banking system and banking institutions in this country which cannot be improved upon in the opinion of this parliament, and that therefore there was little to be gained from a study of our system, or they would say that this government has taken an arbitrary stand, and therefore even if they study our system with a view to trying to improve it there would be no prospect of bringing an improved system into force.
I am also convinced that if we pass this act renewing the bank charters and the banks continue to function as they have been in the past, some of .our industries will be forced to seek other sources to enable them to carry on their business. I do not know that I would be prepared to suggest what might happen in that line, but it would almost seem that they will have to devise something to take the place of money. It is possible that our agriculturists instead of selling grain will go out and sell bonds. It might be a good idea to encourage that, but I do not believe that we should actually make it necessary for them to do so by the imposition of a banking system which evidently has never met their demands at least.
I should also like to make a few remarks about the inefficiency of our present banking system, especially in regard to the banks carrying on their own business. We have very recently had what has often been referred to as the Merchants Bank catastrophe. We have seen some of the managers of that bank tried, and we have seen them whitewashed. We know that that bank lost sev-
(Mr. Kellner.
eral millions of money and the courts have proclaimed that no one was to blame. Now, if there is something the matter with our act so that when a man who has not used due discretion or honesty in handling the funds of the public cannot be convicted under it, I think we should know what it is, and I very much doubt if any member of this House does know wherein the weakness of the act in that respect lies. If it is our criminal code that is at fault, an investigation into that, which we shall probably never have if we renew these charters now for more than one year, would probably give us very valuable information.
It would be still better if an investigation were held to see if our juridical authorities might not be persuaded to at least consider the law in the light that parliament intended. Where the law is ignored entirely you have occurrences like the Merchants Bank catastrophe. If we were to go through another period of stress and some of the other banks were to get into a similar condition, I am a little afraid the managers of those banks would feel they were quite entitled to go ahead and make such disposition of the funds at their command as they saw fit; that there would be no punishment coming to them if they did so. The impression is going abroad that where a large sum of money, well up into the thousands or even into the millions of dollars, is involved there is little need for a man to fear the law; in some way or other he always seems to evade it. On the other hand it is held there is no escape for the offender if the amount lost is insignificant.
One other argument, I think, can be advanced against an extension of these bank charters for ten years, and it can be based on the statement that domination, in the end, will be eliminated. I do not believe that as matters stand we are getting very close to the elimination of that domination. I am convinced that the vast majority of the money which the banks have lent in the last few years has gone to pay interest on debts. Now, I ask you where are matters going to end if it is going to take our entire production to pay the interest on our borrowing? I do not think that anyone will argue that we can keep making fresh loans if it takes more than it is possible to raise in this country of ours to pay the interest on those loans A good deal of evidence was given befoie the committee on Banking and Commerce showing that many of our industries, and in particular that of agriculture, have found it impossible to pay the rate of interest which the banks claim they require in order to

Bank Act
be able to operate. It would seem to me, under all the circumstances, that we have leached this stage: We must either find a better banking system or we are faced with the elimination of agriculture. I believe that is one of the things we should consider veiy seriously before we decide to give the banks a new lease of life for ten years. Personally, I am convinced it would be much more important to the country to have a prosperous farming community, or at least have that community carrying on under decent livable conditions, than to have a dominating banking system in Canada. The present conditions, in my opinion would be greatly ameliorated if the government would only be brave for awhile and see if it were not possible to, at least, bring about a reduction in the interest we are compelled to pay. It is all very well to talk about a safe banking system, or a safe monetary system, but if that system gets "too safe" it is liable to become very weak. I think that fact was pretty well demonstrated at some of our committee meetings.
Now, the Bank Act, as I understand it, is in reality a contract between the banking institutions and the people and, I suppose, it is more or less assumed that this agreement is reasonably fair to both parties. But many hon. members will recall that there were quite a number of lobbyists operating in connection with the Banking and Commerce committee, and I think, perhaps, it is not too strong a statement to say that these lobbyists were encouraged, and probably paid for their attendance, by the banking institutions. It therefore seems scarcely possible-when one party is represented by active lobbyists, and the other party is left unrepresented-that the agreement arrived at can be absolutely fair. In conclusion I desire to say that I shall support the amendment, and that in my opinion it would be a fatal mistake to renew these charters at the present time for a longer period than one year.

After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before I proceed to the few
general remarks I am about to make, I should like to pay a moment's attention to the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), and I do so very deferentially because of the unfailing tolerance that the hon. gentleman always shows towards opinions that differ from his. But in his remarks he showed
himself to be under some misapprehension as to our motives in taking up the time of the committee in further debating the Bank Act. I do not think we are anxious for publicity; at least we are not more anxious for it than other people are to avoid it. Our motive is pretty straightforward, and it is simply that due attention should be given to a very critical matter, I might say matters. I was referring more particularly to the one I had personally in mind. The hon. member implied that the Bank Act had already received a very thorough and searching revision, but I wish to take exception to that. The investigation into the Bank Act up to the present time has been of a rather perfunctory character with the exception of the part played by the small group representing this corner of the House. The word "revision" is almost a misnomer. What we have had has been a rather monotonous re-affirmation of the sanctity, inviolability and general unimpeachability of the Bank Act of this country.
I do not think we have had a very earnest and whole-hearted inquiry into the weaknesses and the failings, the demonstrated failings, of our present Bank Act; that in spite of the fact that in the last decade we have had one of the most unprecedented bank failures in the history of our country. The fact that we have had such a failure seems to have had very little influence upon this House. This House, or at any rate, a large section of it, is counting upon the shortness of the memory of the public. It is adopting the wisdom of the proverb that instructs us to "let sleeping dogs lie." I believe the memory of the public is short. I think it all too soon forgets the wrongs and injustices that take place from time to time. The lessons go unlearned. The people are unprofited by these things that hurt their interests, that inflict serious wounds upon the body politic. They forget them all too soon, and I am sorry to say that our statesmen and members of parliament exploit that weakness with regard to the public. I am not saying this on the strength of my own judgment, for it is well known that the press of this country, after the trials in connection with the Merchants Bank case, were clamorous for some kind of public inquiry, some efficient investigation. Those demands were widespread and unequivocal. Yet here we are almost at the end of this session; this matter has been smoothed over, passed over, and the proposition is to let it go.
I do not intend to take up the time of the committee, but I wish to make my earnest protest against this action of the House. Some one will say that attempts have been made to remedy the act so that these things
Bank Act

will not occur again. I want to give the Finance Minister, who is responsible for the amended act, due credit for a sincere attempt to remedy the act, so far as it can be remedied by words; but I do not think the act can be remedied in that way. One scrap of paper cannot amend another scrap of paper. The old section was just as plain, as explicit and as watertight as ingenuity could make it. You can pick out any one of the Ten Commandments, and you will find that it is not more explicit than the old section, but in spite of that fact $10,000,000 disappeared. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that an act of parliament that has a hole in it big enough to allow $10,000,000 to slip through needs, not merely to be tinkered in the gingerly fashion we have attempted to amend it, but requires a new bottom, and an overhauling through and through. I do not think we have attempted to learn from the things that have befallen us. We have been bitten once, and we are still as bold as ever. We have not only left the stable door open but it seems to me we are about to open the paddock gate too. By our passivity we are inviting a recurrence of this affair.
Just a word on another phase of this question. I imagine that the side of the Merchants Bank question that is most interesting to the public has to do with the transactions that occurred previous to the false returns that were the basis for an action in court. It was not so much the lending as the borrowing that interested the public. One paper, I remember, came out very boldly in this regard, and made the suggestion that behind the Merchants Bank case there was all the sinister evil of stock exchange gambling. I think it was the Finance Minister who assured us some time ago that there was no mystery about the Merchants Bank case. It was just bad loans-injudicious loaning. I wish to say that I think he has left out the most important phase of the question. It was not the injudicious loaning that was the important thing, but it was the judicious borrowing-the very judicious borrowing, I would say-and the public has a right to know something at any rate of the influences that so worked upon our bank officials as to make them commit the error which they committed, f you like to call it an error. I would not characterize this borrowing as being in any sense criminal, although some of the public papers went so far as to suggest that it was almost verging upon criminality. I do not want to go so far as that. It reminds me of the reproaches that Reynard, the fox, made when the cat charged him with stealing a goose. He said, "Do not say 'steal' pussy, 
that is not courteous or kind; but say that I obtained it through my superior ability." Well, there is a lot of that kind of acquisition going on unknown to the public, and I think the public has a right to know the methods by which people can get into the inside of our banks and get away with astounding sums of money, as they did in this case. We have heard a lot about the business acumen of our bank presidents and our bank directors; but how can they hold up their heads again before the world and claim that they are supermen in all things that pertain to sound finance when, under their very noses, people entered into their institutions and took out $10,000,000? I am sometimes amazed at the futility of the ordinary bank robber, the man who undertakes all the risk attached to an ordinary bank robbery, where he breaks into the bank in the dead of night, fully armed, ready to take all the consequences. I wonder at men being content to go on in the old-fashioned way doing these things and taking all the risk, when this other kind of thing goes on, and when men go into financial institutions and take out all this wealth, get away with it and nothing is said.
With reference to those false returns, the courts of this country-and we do not need to reflect upon their decision-said that these returns were not false, but that they were involuntarily misleading. The disappearance of all this money occurred in a fit of absence of mind. It was done without anybody being consciously blameworthy. It was not a fault, or a criminal action. It was an involuntary action, misleading, it is true, but misleading in an involuntary sense. Now the public's interest in a thing of that kind is clear. It does not matter to the public whether it was voluntary or involuntary. It is dangerous just the same. It makes no difference whether it was done wilfully or not, the same amount of money is missing. And this is what we are concerned about. It seems to me that the only way of preventing a recurrence of such a scandal is for parliament to see to it that in future the government make its own returns. I am not going to enter into all the threadbare arguments against outside inspection-arguments which appeal only to those who represent our big financial interests and who are jealous of having their privileges inquired into. The view taken by the average man in the street is that the government should be able to make certain that this sort of thing does not go on in our banks. The evidence before the courts showed that two government officials after only two days' inspection of the books of the

Bank Act
Merchants Bank discovered that millions of dollars were missing. We are not asking for any elaborate inspection and audit, we are not asking that all the petty accounts of the myriad branches should be investigated. We are simply asking that an efficient man in the pay of the government should have the right to scan the ledgers at the main offices of these banks and at their more important branches and so ascertain the actual condition of affairs. Common sense would dictate that such a man, almost by a single glance, could tell if there was serious mismanagement. I think that is what the public expects and what it would demand if this question could only be kept before the public mind, for, as I said before, the public has a knack of forgetting these important things and waiting until the next financial disaster occurs before rousing itself to renewed action.
Now, a word in regard to the merger of the Merchants Bank with the Bank of Montreal. In announcing this merger the Minister of Finance regretted the trend of the concentration of financial control in a few hands, and yet he saw no alternative but to impose this merger upon the country. He proposed to cure one evil by inflicting another. Our banking system had been affected, so to speak, with scarlet fever, and he straightway inoculated it with typhoid in the hope of eradicating the first disease. He stated that we were passing through serious times, that the public mind is fickle, and therefore we must not hesitate or delay but must plunge into this recognized evil in order to escape another. Some of our newspapers strongly criticized-not the action of the Minister of Finance, but the action that instigated the merger, and one prominent journal called it a cowardly action not justified by the circumstances.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not think the Minister of Finance-and he is about the only spokesman for the forces of hurry in this House; there are not very many others who are bold enough to stand up and plead for rushing the Bank Act through-I do not think the minister advances any other argument but that of stability. And to stabilize has become characteristic of him. We know that he has stabilized our tariff. Now he proposes to stabilize our financial system.
We have seen a very significant combination of forces brought about in this House to prevent us in this quarter securing what we consider to be a very reasonable delay in the revision of the act. It is said that trouble makes strange bed-fellows. Well, sometimes even the unfounded anticipation of trouble
has the same effect. We have had the spectacle of Liberal members joining hands with Conservative members in trying to thwart the very reasonable desires of the Progressive party. The other night I saw what I thought was the extreme of incompatibility -a lion riding on the back of a mule; but during the progress of this act through parliament we have seen an equally strange sight-the Conservative party in an "unholy alliance" with the Liberal party in an attempt to block free discussion of the Bank Act.
That is a shame.

The trouble is you do not feel the shame. To me it is strange how enthusiasms evaporate in this House. Last session when the Progressives were not saying very much about inadequate discussion of the Bank Act, we had some very eloquent speeches from the Conservative side urging a thorough discussion of the act in view of the Merchants Bank fiasco, and the House will pardon me for reading at length a few extracts from last year's Hansard because I know hon. members will find them very interesting. At that time a prominent member on the Conservative side said:
Let me turn to another subject that has not been mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. I refer to the Bank Act. I understand tliat next year is really the time for the amendment of that act. I was of the opinion that it should have been amended this year to conform with the practice of the past, but in that perhaps I am mistaken. Whether that be the case or not, however, I think that the Banking and Commerce committee might very properly make a careful examination this year into the workings of the Bank Act, that is to say, into some of its evident weaknesses. I am not one of those who subscribe to the statement that our banking system has not proven workable, or that it is an unsuccessful system which is not in the best interests of the people. I am not ready to endorse the remarks of the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) made this afternoon-statements which seemed to me with great facility and despatch to dispose of this great problem with a complacency that one might well envy, if, indeed, the remarks of the hon. gentleman could bring about a solution of the problem. I believe that our banking system is, in the main, a sound one; it is one of the best systems in the world. Nevertheless, we have to consider the incident of the Merchants Bank during the past few months to realize that there are weaknesses, or, shall I say, loopholes in the Bank Act, and that it is necessary, if not to reconstruct, at least to amend it, so as to render impossible a recurrence of the failure of the Merchants Bank.
And the word "failure" is not mine.
Perhaps that word is too strong; at all events, let me say the incident of the Merchants Bank. For instance, the Merchants Bank directorate or management must have made false returns to the Department of Finance for several months before the crash came. I do not see how the returns that they did make could approach accuracy in view of the sudden collapse, or partial collapse that confronted us. If it
Bank Act

is true, as I surmise-and I think the evidence strongly supports the assumption-that the bank made false returns, then this parliament ought to know it, and I believe that the Banking and Commerce committee should summon before it the management, the president and any other officials of the Merchants Bank, who might throw light on the matter, in order that parliament might be fully seized of all the steps which led up to this very regrettable incident in the banking life of this country. Furthermore, the Banking committee could very well make this examination for the purpose of preparing amendments to the Bank Act, when it comes up for general revision next year.
Whose speech is my hon. friend quoting from?

The hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), I think. I might supplement that by a quotation from another hon. member on the Conservative side of the House, just to show that we on this side are not doing anything at the present time that need be taken as unwonted or extraordinary; we are taking an attitude which was taken by others last session. Another hon. member said:
In conclusion, I want to refer to three or four other matters which I think should be mentioned in this debate, because this is the only opportunity we have of doing so under the rules of the House.
This is the utterance of a member for Toronto-one of the greatest financial centres in Canada-who was specially interested in this subject.	[DOT]
'If there ever was in this country an act that needed overhauling, it is the much-heralded Bank Act. Some newspapers are beginning to wonder whether there is to be one law for the rich and another for the poor in this country.
I think it is necessary for me to say again that this is the utterance of a Conservative member, otherwise the committee might think I was quoting from the speech of one of the representatives of labour.
I have read, in some very reputable newspapers, in Canada, articles referring to some people who stole $8,000 out of a bank, and some other poor fellow who took $1.25 out of a postal envelope. The people who stole $8,000 got a life sentence because they robbed the bank with violence; the poor postman, on a small salary without bonus, who took $1.25 out of an envelope, was sent down. This matter of the Merchants Bank should not be left to any superior or high court judge of the province of Quebec; or the Appellate division either; there should be an independent inquiry by the High Court of parliament and no whitewash. We should find out whether we have a Bank Act, whether it is a mere scrap of paper or not, and whether the monthly returns made by the bank to the minister are scraps of paper or not. I believe the losses will run to twelve or thirteen million dollars before they get through. What protection has the investor, the stockholder? I know one man in my city who has started to sell out every dollar's worth of stock he has in some small banks. When I asked him the reason, he said that he was very doubtful if, in some of the smaller banks, the shareholders have the protection which they should have. This parliament should be big enough to go into the whole

question of the Merchants Bank. The banks have been allowed to increase their note circulation; they have been given many special privileges, and a thorough inquiry should be made into the whole matter. The House and the country expect us to do our duty in this matter. Where do the Progressives stand upon it?
I notice that the hon. gentleman is not in the House to-night to say where he stands.
Whose speech was that?

I have difficulty in remembering where these hon. gentlemen come from; that was the hon. member for North Toronto, I believe. Well, why has this enthusiasm evaporated to such an extent that the battle is left entirely to us? I can understand why hon. members on the other side have not expressed themselves, but I cannot understand why the enthusiasts to my right should have dropped this matter and left us to wage the fight alone. Now,-

Will my hon. friend permit me? He has quoted at some length from a speech I made last year. May I point out to him and to the committee that that speech was delivered before the prosecutions were launched against the officials of the Merchants Bank, and it was with the distinct understanding that these prosecutions were going on that I dropped a motion that I put on the order paper last year. Any further discussion would have done a grave injustice to those who were being prosecuted in the criminal courts of the country. If, as is common to a committee of parliament, evidence were brought forward in a loose manner while this case was pending, the parties would hardly have a. fair chance in the courts; accordingly, this matter was not proceeded with last year. The prosecution having been held and a very complete threshing out of the whole problem having taken place, the needs presented there do not stand this year as they did at that time before any prosecutions were commenced.
The hon. gentleman's explanation is all right but I think he must have been aware that the prosecution was pending while he uttered those words.

It had not been launched; and the Minister of Finance if he were in his seat, would bear me out, I am quite sure. It was subsequent to that speech and subsequent to the placing on the order paper of a resolution to refer the whole question to the Banking and Commerce committee that the knowledge, even the preliminary intimation, that the prosecutions would be launched was brought to my attention.

My point is that the hon. gentleman must have known that this thing was going to the courts.

I beg to correct my hon. friend; I have done so once. I knew absolutely nothing about it until it was conveyed to me subsequent to both the speech and the placing of the resolution on the order paper. I consented to let the resolution stand for the reasons I have mentioned.

Well, I am bound to accept the hon. gentleman's word in regard to his lack of knowledge, but in regard to the prospective action in the courts, if my memory is correct the knowledge was pretty well diffused throughout the country that the Finance Minister had decided that this thing should be investigated in the courts. However-

I must correct my hon. friend. I cannot allow him indirectly to impute lack of accuracy to my statement. What I say is this, and I state it again most positively; that the prosecutions were not launched, there were no intimations to the public that they were to be launched, until subsequent to both the speech and the resolution going on the order paper. If the Minister of Finance were in his seat I would appeal to him for permission to make a statement that would prove that beyond per-adventure. I ask my hon. friend not to impute inaccurate statements to me, even indirectly.

I assure my hon. friend that I have no intention of doing that. But I quoted from his speech in good faith rather to show his enthusiasm in the matter last session, and I think that part of his speech shows that he had great enthusiasm. The point of his interruption is valuable only if the action in the courts fulfilled the earnest desire he expressed in that speech and I think it will be very hard for him to contend that it did.
Now, I want to refer again to the course which the Minister of Finance has taken. I wish to make the charge of inconsistency against the Finance Minister with as light a hand as I possibly can, but in the light of his actions when the revision of the Bank Act was up some ten or twelve years ago I think it will be difficult for him to escape that imputation at least to some slight extent. The revision of the Bank Act was up before this House in the sessions of 1909 and 1910, when our present Minister of Finance occupied that same office. Early in the session in answer to Mr. Borden, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) said with respect to the Bank Act revision, "This matter was very well advanced," and would be presented "early this session."
Later in answer to a question he said, "It is contemplated to provide a Bank Act this session." On February 14 of the same session, in reply to Mr. Foster, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) said that he was bringing forward an act which "would not be much longer delayed." In reply to Mr. Foster later on he said that the act was in an advanced condition but that all would depend on other business. If the session was protracted, it would be that session; if not, the next session. Towards the end of the session, in reply to Mr. Emmerson, he said that there would not be sufficient time that session. The next year the opposition got very clamorous and the bill was introduced on December 15,
1910,	in the early part of the session, but was not proceeded with until March 31 the following spring, when Mr. Lennox asked for action. The contention of Mr. Lennox was that some very serious bank failures had taken place during the decade. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) replied:
If circumstances make it necessary to bring in a temporary bill carrying the banks over for another year, I think no harm would be done. A little further time will not be to the disadvantage of any interest concerned. ... I do not think that any great public interest will suffer.
Mr. Foster also urged strongly that the government proceed with the bill. On April 4,
1911,	the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) further put off the matter, and on May 11 of that year he announced that a bill would be introduced for extension of the bank charters for one year. But they were not fated to proceed with the bill, for the next session found others in possession, and in the Hansard of that next session I find that the new government adopted the same delaying tactics. Mr. Lemieux early in the session inquired whether action would be taken that session, and Mr. Borden replied that it was simply a matter of time. Later on Mr. Macdonald also inquired, and he too was put off. So I think that the House cannot claim that this group on this side of the House is asking for anything that is unprecedented. We are asking for a course that was pursued at the last revision of the Bank Act, and the delay that we are asking is only for one session, and for a very good reason. On that former occasion the revision was delayed from session to session without any good reason except the urgency of other business. Now as a young member of this House, as a politician very much in the green, I find we have to go back
Bank Act

at least ten years in the lives of our prominent public men to find out what is proper to do to-day. We find out what they did about ten years ago, and then we go and do the opposite and we get the unanimous approval of this House. I wish to put that on record, not to charge the Finance Minister with any grave inconsistency because he may have justified himself, he surely will have justified himself in his own mind for the transformation of his conduct between now and then, and again I want to allude to the distinct courtesy and tolerance of the Minister of Finance as exercised towards us as we have endeavoured in our inexperienced way to put these objections of ours before him. The hon. minister kicks us downstairs with such infinite grace that you might think he was helping us up, and I for one have no objection to the way in which he has met our objections. I am sorry he should be such a lone mouthpiece in this unjustifiable policy of rush and hurry. I am sorry there are not more articulate exponents of that mystical doctrine of "get this thing through as quick as you can," for no ascertainable reason. I think it is very significant that he should be left alone to bear the burden of this contention.
I want to say in concluding that although we may have gone about this thing in a somewhat unrestrained manner at times, yet we have been acting in good faith and with the belief that we were carrying out the dictates of public opinion, and I believe that public opinion will sustain us in the action we have taken. I think it will be very hard for both the other parties to explain to the public why they carried this thing through as they have done against the reiterated protests from the group on this side of the House.

Mr. Chairman,
I rise to protest not so much against the Bank Act, for I was not a member of the Banking and Commerce committee, but for the purpose of protesting against extending without further consideration the bank charters for another ten years. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have mentioned the muddle into which the Merchants Bank got, and most of us here, particularly those from the province of Ontario, will remember that it was only a few years before that the Farmers Bank failed, and I really believe that that bank was in a bigger muddle than the Merchants Bank. Some of the managers of that institution although they had condemned themselves were let go by the courts. One of them skipped out of this country just as soon as the failure took place

and was hounded round and found at last in the city of Chicago, I believe. He was brought back to this country and haled before the courts, and a verdict of not guilty was brought in about one minute before the man passed into the other world, and no man in this House or any other house can make me believe that he was not guilty.
The same kind of thing took place in connection with the Merchants Bank, and I rise to protest against extending the charters of these banks for another ten years until those men are brought before the bar of this House. My hon. friend from Nelson has covered the case of the Merchants Bank pretty fully, and I shall detain the House only for a few minutes to ask the Minister of Finance if he thinks the people of this country are going to stand for seeing millions of dollars squandered by these institutions and the men responsible let go scot-free. Do the bankers of Canada think they have special privileges entitling them to squander that money? Let me cite a few of the items showing the manner in which the money has been squandered. Loans to the extent of two millions were made to the officers of the bank for the purchase of automobiles and fancy homes. Little of this money came back. Advances to the total of four and a half millions were made to one stock broking firm that engaged in gambling and exploitation, and only $500,000 of it came back. To protect a debt, owed by one of the manufacturing firms amounting to $65,000 a total of $1,300,000 was advanced and $1,000,000 was lost. This accounts for probably only one-half of the total amount that was squandered, I do not think I am using too strong a term when I say "squandered." The details of the other half are probably even more shocking than the ones I have mentioned, but I do not see any advantage in enumerating any more of them and occupying the time of the House unduly. Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to enter my protest against making such advances. As I have not studied the Bank Act, not being a member of the committee, I shall merely enter my protest on that phase of the subject and leave the matter there.

I should like to make just one observation as to the point raised by the hon. member for Nelson. He drew the attention of the House to a statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) last year in which he distinctly recommended that some of the officers of the late Merchants Bank should have been brought before the House, or before one of its committees, to give information. When

Bank Act
this fact was brought to his attention by the hon. member (Mr. Bird) he defended himself on the ground that at that time the prosecution had not been taken. Subsequently it was undertaken and therefore he sees no reason to make the same request this year. Now, I want to submit to him, and to the House, that the information which was elicited during the trial is entirely irrelevant to the purposes for which we would wish to have that information in this House. Therefore, I contend that the defence which my hon. friend put in is entirely outside the point. The information that we wish to get is not that connected with the particular indictments brought at the trial, it is information of a very much wider character. I consider the defence of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre in that respect is very weak, and I am sorry that he has not joined with us this year in renewing the demand that he made last year.

As one of the western representatives I want to take this opportunity of placing myself on record in favour of the amendment. A very significant feature in connection with the consideration of the Bank Act this year, was the fact that thousands of representative citizens throughout the country were consulted by letter and asked for their opinions as to the revision of the act. The replies received would indicate that people throughout Canada believe there is a direct relationship between the credit system or the banking system of this country and the recovery of the agricultural industry. I think it is only fair to Canadian agriculturists to state that they have put forth almost superhuman efforts in an endeavour to solve this problem, apart from federal aid. In this regard it is well to remember what has been done in several provinces of Canada. Farm loans, rural credits, and provincial banks have been established in an effort to meet the situation and, as far as western Canada is concerned, have proved inadequate only because of the limit of capital at the disposal of these institutions. It is owing to the fact that the people have realized their limitations in this respect that they now appeal to the federal government to come to their assistance. And Mr. Chairman, even though a more adequate system cannot be evolved in the immediate future a free and frank discussion of the whole situation would tend to allay suspicion, and would also tend to strengthen the hands of the banks themselves. It would restore the confidence of the people in the banks, and great institutions such as these cannot be carried on successfully
for any length of time unless they enjoy the confidence of the people. For the reasons I have given I intend" to support the amendment.

I wish to say
a word or two with respect to the remarks that have been made by hon. gentlemen since the committee commenced the consideration of the bill. It is not necessary for hon. gentlemen opposite to defend their motives in criticizing the measure. I am sure ample opportunity will be given to every hon. gentleman to make any observations he desires on the bill, or to suggest any amendment which he wishes between now and the time the measure will come from the committee. I do say however that when hon. gentlemen undertake to say that the revision of the Bank Act should not have been proceeded with they should give reasons for that statement, and the reasons should be substantial, they should be reasoned, and they should be based upon something, whether that something is strong, weak, or indifferent. Hon. gentlemen who have spoken this afternoon have not, in my judgment, given reasons for a delay in the revision of the Bank Act.
One hon. member, just a moment ago, referred to the fact that in 1911 a bill for the revision of the Bank Act was introduced and was deferred. Hon. gentlemen need only to recall the political incidents of that year to appreciate what happened. It was the session of parliament in which the Reciprocity treaty with the United States came before the country as a political issue. The session of parliament closed rather hurriedly, and the whole country was en-9 p.m. gaged in a political contest over that particular issue. The government of the day was defeated and in 1912 the new ministry asked for a delay in the matter of the revision of the Bank Act. That was quite natural because the new government, with the many duties which constitutionally devolved upon them, would expect the country to justify them in asking for an extension of time. Accordingly, in 1912 an act was passed extending the term of the Bank Act. The reason for not proceeding with the revision of the Bank Act then was a very good reason, and it proved satisfactory to the country at the time.
Hon. gentlemen say that many demands have been made for delay in the revision of the Bank Act during the present session. I heard it said this afternoon that there was a body of men in my own province of Nova Scotia favourable to delaying the revision of the act. I venture to say that if you can-
Bank Act

vassed the entire population of the provinces you would have difficulty in finding twenty-one out of the whole half million who had so expressed themselves. I believe a resolution was passed at some farmers' convention. I had the privilege of inquiring of two prominent persons who were present at that convention and they could not even recall that it was considered. That resolution must have come before the convention in the most informal and perfunctory manner.
There were only fifteen there anyway.

My hon. friend from Lunenburg suggests that there were only fifteen present, but I think there were more. But I venture to say that in the Maritime provinces there was no body of public opinion favourable to a postponement of the revision of the Bank Act. They desire reasonable, fair and proper amendments to it, of course, as do the people of every other section of Canada. There is no reason for asking for a delay in parliament doing its duty, namely extending the bank charters of this country when such charters expire at the end of the decennial period. The duty rests upon parliament and upon every hon. member to extend those charters, and they should be extended except for some strong, substantial reasons which as yet have not been given to parliament, nor to the Banking and Commerce committee. Again I venture to give as a reason why parliament should insist upon the renewal of the charters at the present time, the fact that the whole banking system has been challenged and foolish, dangerous substitutes have been suggested. I think it is wise that parliament and the country should express their disapproval of those suggestions. Hon. members say that we are rushing this *bill through parliament.
Hear, hear.

An hon. member opposite in very subdued tones says "hear, hear," and I fancy that the tone in which that interjection was uttered is an indication that he did not feel very strongly in that direction himself. So far as I know, no effort on the part of the government, or of the committee, or of any hon. member has been made to rush this bill through the House. It was a long while in the committee. The Bank Act itself was well considered, and before it went to the committee it has had the consideration of the Department of Finance. Important amendments appeared in the bill before it went to the committee, and the House approved the bill as amended before
]Mr. Bancroft.l
it was sent to the committee. It was considered in the committee, section by section, and clause by clause, and no very important amendments were suggested by any hon. members opposite. I commend them for their energy and the attention they gave to the bill while it was being considered by the committee, but I say in all frankness and kindliness that they did not propose any amendment of a substantial nature to the bill. It is true that other important questions came up; but as regards the Bank Act itself, members of the Progressive party who were members of the Banking committee, made no very serious and important suggestions, and if amendments of that character were made, the committee gave ample and due consideration to them. How long do hon. members think a bill of this character should be considered in parliament or in committee? Are we going to sit month after month, year after year, decade after decade? How long is it going to take hon. members to make up their minds as to what a bill means, and what their decision will be about the matter? We would have no laws anywhere if hon. members engaged in legislative halls were to say: "You must not rush; we must have time to consider." Everybody, I think, has had ample opportunity to make any suggestion and to propose any amendment that was of any value.
We have in Canada a banking system which has been in existence since confederation and which is known as the branch bank system I think it has functioned well and successfully in this country. Like everything else it may have its weak points, and it is our duty as parliamentarians to eradicate those weak features if we can put our fingers upon them. But we must have a Bank Act, because if we did not have some banking system under the authorization of the statutes of our country, commerce and trade could not be carried on and everything in this country would stop. I think, speaking generally, every hon. member feels that our banking system on the whole is a pretty sound system, and that it has operated pretty well in the past. It stood the strain of the war test as well as any other banking system in the world. I think our' bank managers and directors deserve credit for the management of Canadian banks during the war period, and it should be said of them, that they came through that ordeal in as good shape as did banks of any other country in the world.
Hon. members have referred to the Merchants Bank failure, and they spoke of money having been lost. They talk as if by some act of parliament, the recurrence of such a

Bank Act
thing should be prevented. Bank failures cannot be prevented by legislation any more than the commission of crime can be prevented by criminal laws. Even the Ten Commandments to which one horu member referred this evening are violated though they came to the sons of men amid the lightnings and thunders of Mount Sinai. It is perfect nonsense to think that you can eliminate human weakness, errors in human judgment, by acts of parliament. Of course we must do everything we possibly can to prevent bank failures in the future, but I do not hesitate to say that they will occur in the future. After all a bank is in essence no different from a crossroads country grocery store. The country store sells general groceries, or something or another, and the bank merchandisers' credit. There is quite a contrast, it is true, as to the exact character of the businesses, but after all each buys and sells something. As long as human nature is what it is, we shall have failures at the country cross-roads store and in banks in Canada. To say that because the Merchants Bank of Canada failed, we should delay re-enactment of Canadian bank charters, is reasoning that I cannot understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Merchants Bank did not fail.

The Minister
of Finance reminds me, and it is true, that the Merchants Bank of Canada did not fail. They decided to go out of business, as many concerns and corporations are deciding to do to-day and will to-morrow in these distressing days in commercial life the world over. The Merchants Bank extended their loans too freely. Somebody made a mistake; the management made mistakes, and in my judgment some of their mistakes are not very easily condoned.

Will the hon. member say
whether he knows or does not know why the Merchants Bank failed?
Because in the course of business they lost a certain amount of their assets by weak loans. They became weak, just in the same manner as ordinary business concerns become weak and fail.

Will the hon. member
admit that they failed?

There is not
much use in discussing that. I said a moment ago that they did not fail, and as a matter of fact and of law, they did not fail. The noteholders were paid. The depositors were paid. The shareholders possibly suffered a loss in
the value of their shares, but by their vote they agreed to the sale of the assets of the bank. The Department of Finance instituted criminal proceedings against two officers of that bank. After trial in the courts of the province of Quebec these men were acquitted. What more could be done? How ineffective it would be to have an investigation in the Banking and Commerce committee. Would there be any tribunal as ill-fitted in all Canada as parliament to investigate a failure of that kind? We have had bank failures in the past and the country was satisfied with the public inquiry or the investigations in the courts concerning these particular failures. I think in connection with some of the bank failures preceding that of the Merchants Bank some bank managers went to penitentiary. That did not happen in the case of the failure of the Merchants Bank. But I ask hon. members, what more could be done, and why is it made the basis for the suggestion that we should postpone the further consideration of the Bank Act.
I said a moment ago that very important amendments had been made to this act, and I particularly refer to the new clauses in respect of the shareholders' audit, and to the provisions which require the shareholders' auditors to bring to the knowledge of the directors all the facts which should come before them in connection with the business of the bank. The latter I regard as an important amendment, for if by any audit system you can bring to the attention of the directors the important facts in connection with the business affairs of an institution, particularly its weak and doubtful points, I think you have gone just about as far as you can go in the way of legislation to give security to depositors and shareholders. But if these amendments are not sufficient, further amendments can be made upon the suggestion of any hon. member, and that is our business here while the bill is before the committee.
Reference has been made to the financial conditions of the country, and it is said the present banking system is not of a character to meet effectually the present situation. Many hon. gentlemen in this House fail to distinguish between banking institutions and credit institutions. It was felt by many hon. members in the committee, and I think in the House, that there was possibly a field for some finangjal institution operating between the banks and mortgage corporations which might be filled by some financial institution, call it what you will. We generally refer to them as rural credit associations. This particular form of credit is being tried in the
Bank Act

United States to-day. In Europe we find they usually operate under the name of some cooperative association, and splendid things have been done there, and I do hope that some day soon we may have them in Canada. The conditions in western Canada, I admit, are deplorable. Therefore, the minds of many hon. members opposite belonging to the Progressive party are centred upon the conditions prevailing in their own particular section of Canada. We all appreciate that. In some sections of the province of Alberta, where they have had a failure in crops for three years, the conditions are particularly distressing, but that is not due to any economic law or any weakness in the banking institutions of this country. Nobody on earth is to blame for that condition, and if blame is to be attached, hon. gentlemen opposite will have to go into another sphere to find who is to blame. The chief difficulty in the western country to-day is that many farmers overborrow. That is admitted. That has been admitted by pretty nearly every hon. member from the western provinces who took part in the deliberations of the committee on Banking and Commerce. I understand this admission was made frequently by western men before another committee. The real problem in the western provinces to-day-at least in one of them, and possibly in two of them-is to devise some scheme by which the present indebtedness to banks, to mortgage corporations, to merchants and others could be lifted from the shoulders of the people and spread over a long period of years. That probably concerns the farmers of the West more to-day than the question of rural credits for the future. The member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) said to-day that several schemes were presented before the Banking committee which are not to be found here. Well, there were some schemes presented to the Banking and Commerce committee, and some of them were very fantastic.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

Does the hon. member think it is fair for him to make a lot of statements about what was presented in committee, but were never considered in committee? He is only offering his opinion, which is as good as anybody else's, but no better. He is not speaking for the commitfee in that regard. The committee came to no conclusion on that question.

Why did the hon. gentleman not make his remarks to the

hon. member behind him (Mr. Bird) when he was stating to the committee that these suggestions were not incorporated in the bill, and urging that as a ground for delaying the consideration of the bill?

If the hon. member who spoke on this side of the House made a mistake in referring to them, does the hon. gentleman think he is doing any better by making these statements concerning matters which were never considered in committee?
I do not think 1 have made any mistake in the statements I have made, and I am not apologizing to the hon. gentleman at all. I was perfectly within my right in making the remarks I did.
The hon. member has not answered my question.

I do not propose to discuss the schemes of Mr. Douglas, or Mr. Bevington, or Mr. Fisher, because this is not an opportune time. I think the opportunity will come later. A great many other remarks have been made since this bill was taken up by the committee this afternoon. I thought it desirable to make a few observations regarding some of the criticisms which were made, but I do wish to say that I think, if hon. gentlemen are serious in urging a postponement of the consideration of this bill and its enactment, really some more substantial reasons should be given. I am not objecting to the discussion or criticism. I have been merely attempting to answer some of the criticisms, and I trust the committee will soon see fit to proceed with the bill.

Mr. Chairman, I was not a member of the Banking committee, nor did I attend the sessions of that committee with the regularity that would entitle me to pose as an authority on the subject matter in the discussion of which we are now engaged. However, there is an impression in my mind that the revision of the Bank Act this year received consideration equal to, if not greater than, the consideration accorded any previous revision. The members of the Banking committee met regularly, worked strenuously, and I think the House as a whole is indebted to them for what they have already accomplished.
And yet it seems to me that the demand embodied in the amendment is reasonable- a demand supported by several representative organizations throughout the country, a demand made upon myself by at least twenty or thirty correspondents who have written to me from various sections of the Dominion.

Bank Act
403S
If we penetrate beneath the surface of things in an attempt to answer the question put by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), I think we will discover that this demand is based, first of all, upon a growing tendency in the minds of the Canadian people to-day that our electoral system-that is, the mere mechanical process of holding an election-does not place at the disposal of the people in parliament a sufficient number of specialists to undertake to pass upon a subject so technical, so involved, so abstruse and so far-reaching in its effects as the revision of the Bank Act undoubtedly is. Not only do they lack faith in the ability of their elected representatives, but they are frequently reminded of the limited time at our disposal to undertake and carry to a successful conclusion this Herculean task.
But the senior member for Halifax will remind me that on this occasion specialists were summoned, authorities on banking were brought before the committee and gave evidence, which evidence has been published verbatim. I want to be honest with myself and with hon. members. How many members of the Banking committee have read through that evidence? And of those who have read it through how many fully understand it? But in the last analysis it is not the members of the Banking committee before whom that evidence was taken who are going to be responsible for passing this legislation, it is the hon. members of this Chamber; and again I want to be honest with myself and with hon. members. How many members of this Chamber have read that evidence through? And of those who have done so how many fully understand it? How many could get up here, or before a public audience, and give an intelligent lecture of one hour's duration on the evidence submitted? Has the Prime Minister read that evidence? Doubtless the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has. But, if so, is it not a reasonable request to make of him that he present to this House a brief synopsis of the evidence, showing that in the light of the knowledge that has come to us from the evidence the present measure is the best possible act that can be evolved in the next decade? Again I say, if we penetrate beneath the surface we find that while the people may hav'e faith in the honesty of their elected representatives, they have grave doubts as to their specialized knowledge. That is to say, Democracy's ability to return members to parliament at this time has outdistanced Democracy's ability to discover and return to parliament the right type of man. Hence we have to-day the demand for government by commission. We have a Railway Commission. We have a Civil Service Commission. We have a Board of Grain Commissioners. Last year we had a Royal Commission on Pensions and this year a royal commission inquiring into lake freight rates. I do not know but what the time is rapidly approaching when we shall, in response to this growing demand, have to appoint a commission on banking-a commission on finance. Now, I say to the senior member for Halifax-and I say it in all kindness-that in my humble judgment no government, if it is wise, can afford to treat with impunity and with contempt such tendencies on the part of one people they are seeking to govern. A wise government, a government that is well advised, will take note of such tendencies and attempt to reconcile them with the theory of responsible government.
Turning to the banks for a moment, it would be too much for us to expect that our banking institutions could escape from the storm of criticism, the force of which has been felt by almost every institution within the circle of our national life. The fact that there has been a tendency towards the centralization of financial control, coupled with the fact that our banks have been paying dividends on a normal basis during a period of the most acute financial stringency in Canadian history, has created an impression in the minds of many people that these institutions enjoy advantages and privileges not enjoyed by other institutions in this country.
Then I want to say that this demand is inseparably bound up with the demand for a rural credit scheme. Some scheme or proposal for an extension of rural credits is, in my judgment, indispensably essential if we are to stimulate production in the western sections of this country, which production when stimulated will enable us to meet our financial obligations. Representations have been made to the hon. Minister of Finance with regard to a commission on taxation; it is proposed to hold a conference to which will be invited all the provincial treasurers. It seems to me that that would be an opportune time not only to discuss taxation, it would be an opportune time to discuss the whole problem of rural credit, the funding of farmers' obligations and a thousand and one questions related to that subject. What could be more appropriate than that the present Minister of Finance, after years of service, after his splendid devotion to the cause of duty in this country-what could be more fitting, than

Bank Act

that he, in co-operation with those who are willing to assist him, should in the immediate future evolve some system of rural credit, not a slavish imitation of systems already existing in other countries, but something new, something original, something worthy of Canadian statesmanship, something that will meet our present needs?
So much for the mere economic aspects of the question. When the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) suggests that we are opposed to this bill, he is, not deliberately but unintentionally, misrepresenting our position. We are prepared to support this bill for at least a year, but we are not prepared to support it for a period of ten years, with the information at our disposal. Then, there are other considerations, the least worthy of all-what I would call political considerations. It would scarcely be fair to say that the demand for this postponement comes wholly from western Canada, but I think it is the case that the demand is more pronounced in western Canada, because of the peculiar economic conditions prevailing there. As I listened to the speeches this afternoon 1 thought of the effect those speeches would have upon the present government.
Is the hon. gentleman worrying much about it?

I am not worrying at all. But I wondered if those speeches, broadcasted from one end of this country to the other, would have the effect of rousing the Canadian people and sending thousands to the polls who up to the present have refused to vote. If I thought such speeches had that effect, I would encourage them, but I am inclined to think, and I say it in all seriousness, that utterances of this kind will have a tendency to embitter the Canadian people, to set class against class, to set one section of the country against the other, and to undermine the faith of the Canadian people

that is, the little bit of faith they have left-in political institutions as they exist. I am not persuaded that the present leader of the government has decided to scrap western Canada so far as his future political plans and ambitions are concerned. A gentleman told me to-day he was convinced that the present Prime Minister had pulled down the curtain so far as western Canada was concerned. I am rather inclined to think that the Prime Minister-and I have considerable faith in his sincerity; I wish I had the same faith in his political sagacity-is still willing to make an attempt to unite the different sections that go to constitute the Canadian nation. I do not believe that the Prime 
Minister extracts pleasure from the division that at present exists. But what are the facts? I should be out of order here if I referred to a budget for the creation of which and for the adoption of which the present administration was responsible this year, but I do not think it is an exaggeration to say that that budget, for weal or for woe, caused dismay in the minds of the government's most loyal and devoted followers in the western section of this country. And then they come along with a proposal, the psychological effects of which are going to be tremendous, a proposal and an attitude on the part of the government which if persisted in, and coupled with the speeches that are going to be made, will definitely line the present administration up with the eastern interests. But the Prime Minister says: We have taken a certain position, and we cannot, and maintain our dignity, give way to an irresponsible minority in this House. But I want to remind the present government that if they do not seriously consider the advisability of giving way to a so-called irresponsible minority in this House they are going to be accused oi lining up with an irresponsible minority outside this House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is my friend quoting me when he uses the expression that he has just employed?

I think the Prime Minister misunderstood me. I have not quoted him to-night. I was speaking rhetorically when I said: The present government may say that it cannot, and maintain its dignity, give way to an irresponsible minority in this House. I can only say that if the government do not seriously consider the advisability of giving way to a so-called irresponsible minority in this House they will be accused, they are being accused now, of being dominated by, an irresponsible minority outside this House, namely, the eastern interests. If I were interested in the triumph of mere political parties-and I do not give a continental for the growth or triumph of any party-I would not ask for a better basis upon which to build up the party to which I am attached than the present attitude of the government on the revision of the Bank Act. I do not mean to say that it is a great thing in itself; there is a lot of merit in the argument of the hon. member for Halifax. But if you exercise your imagination and think that men in the paralyzing grip of economic necessity to-day are willing to blame almost anybody in the present crisis-exercise your imagination in that sense, and then think of the future political result.

Bank Act
I am interested in the attitude of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) on this question; I will await his speech with considerable interest. He has much less political sagacity than I give him credit for if he supports the government in putting through for a ten year period this Bank Act, in view of the state of public opinion throughout the country. I have tried to br fair in my remarks; I have tried to be conciliatory; I have no desire to stir up bitterness or to awaken hatreds. I simply submit these considerations to the government for what they are worth, and I wonder if ever yet some compromise could not be reached that would be satisfactory to all concerned, some compromise that would awaken hope in rural Canada that the present administration is at least making an honest, a sincere, a supreme attempt to come to their rescue and to help them out of their present difficulties.

I shall not delay the committee at any great length, but I wish definitely to place myself on record in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) this afternoon. I was not a member of the committee which considered this bill, but I took advantage of any opportunity that presented itself to visit the committee and see it in action. Yet in spite of all that has been said here this evening and what I heard in that committee the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) says that no substantial reason has yet been given for postponing the revision of the Bank Act. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that one of the reasons why the Conservative party went down to defeat in 1921 was because they did not have their finger close enough upon the pulse of public opinion in this country, and the result was that the people placed in office in their stead a new government thinking that it would respond more readily to public opinion. I would like to ask the government now what good reason they can give why this Bank Act revision should not be postponed for another year. Are we asking for anything unreasonable in view of the widespread unrest prevailing throughout Canada to-day?
I might say that our demand is backed up by resolutions from organizations from almost every part of Canada. I shall not weary the House by reading them, but I have _ here resolutions from the government of Manitoba, which is no small organization but represents the people of that whole province, from the government of Alberta, and from the Canadian Council of Agriculture, which represents thousands of organized farmers throughout the
whole of Canada. I have also a letter here signed by Tom Moore, president of the Trades and Labour Congress, which I propose to read:
Dear Sir,-Communications received from a number of our affiliated organizations, including the Trades Councils at Victoria, Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton, Toronto, London, Montreal, St. John and Halifax, all indicate that there is a widespread interest amongst the organized workers regarding the Banking Act.
Labor opinion is strongly favorable to a thorough revision of the Banking Act and entirely opposed to hasty action on such an important matter. It is strongly felt that the mass of evidence submitted to the Banking Committee during this session should be thoroughly analyzed before final decision is reached as to what amendments of benefit to the public could be properly made to the Banking Act and that the present session of parliament is apparently too far advanced to admit of this being done.
We would therefore respectfully urge that the revision of the Banking Act should be postponed until the next session of parliament and would greatly appreciate any assistance you can render to bring about such action.
Is the writer of that letter a director of the Canadian National Railways?
The letter is signed by Tom Moore, president, and P. M. Draper, secretary-treasurer, of the Trades and Labour Congress.
Mr. Moore was before the committee and he never suggested that the revision of the act be postponed. Furthermore he said he had nothing to propose by way of an amendment.

Here, of course, Mr. Moore is speaking for organized labour throughout Canada, and his letter speaks for itself. 1 am not going to argue with the hon. gentleman as to Mr. Moore's views, but I have his letter here above his own signature. One of the reasons we in western Canada especially have for postponing the revision of this Bank Act is the lack of confidence that a great many of our farmers have in our banking system as it exists at the present time. I have here one of our farm papers containing a lengthy article headed "Financing the Farmer." It was put out by the superintendent of the Rural Credits branch of the Merchants Bank before that institution went out of existence. I shall quote only one short sentence:
The farmer who takes his banker into his confidence at all times and under all conditions is making satisfactory progress, and he seldom finds it necessary to seek credit outside the bank to carry on his season's undertakings.
We have had advertisements in our farm papers out in that country along this line:
Bank Act

If you are sick, you go to your doctor for medical advice. If you are in legal difficulties you go to your lawyer. When in financial trouble, why not go to your banker? In this very article it says, "Place your confidence in your banker." I should just like to point out what happened through a man placing confidence in a banker. It is a case that happened in my own district involving an immigrant, one of the finest type that has ever landed in this country. He came from the Jersey islands and was worth considerable money, just the class of settler we are all anxious to see in Canada. He came over and settled in the town of Sedgewick. He went to his banker and placed his full confidence in him, and the result was that on the advice of that banker this settler placed $10,000 in a partnership which was in a very unstable condition. Just to prove that this partnership was in an unstable condition when this man invested his $10,000 in it, I wish to read a letter from the general manager of the Merchants Bank at Montreal which was produced at the trial, and just here I might say that our head bankers often claim that they are not quite responsible for all that the branch managers may do or say. This letter from the general manager of the bank at Montreal goes on to say, speaking of the condition this partnership was in at the time this immigrant invested his money in it:
The inspector suggests that J. Burn has Mr. B. mesmerized, and we think you too. This account is on anything but a satisfactory basis and we want it cleaned up without delay. You say it is impossible to confirm our figures representing wheat, oats, flax, and barley, covered by the bank's pledges, but it is your business to know that the commodities are there.
The door is wide open for perpetration of fraud, and we have seen it happen so often. On the lines of the authorized credit we shall not object, but you have given double the amount we have authorized. Bring it within $10,000 without delay and do not arrogate so much authority again. There is evidence in your liability list that Burn is getting into deep water. Send us a statement of the grain covered by the bank's pledges after you have seen it, obtain also a statement of stored grain and ask Burn to explain to you how he proposes to separate and identify the two classes of grain on hand.
I want to call particular attention to the last paragraph:
If you don't get this account into line quickly I will relieve you of the management. Note that. Now get to work.
This manager got to work, and he was responsible for getting this settler freshly landed in Canada, and who had placed his confidence in that bank manager, to invest $10,000 in that partnership which inside of one year was in such a condition that it was wound up. I want to say that this new

settler holds a very bitter feeling against the banks in western Canada in consequence. He sued the bank for fraudulent misrepresentation, and in summing up the judge said that it was not a matter of justice; he had to administer the law, and that the bank took shelter under an old law dating back as far as 1826. He said: "The advice was given verbally and not in writing, and therefore damages could not be recovered."
We heard Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor, who is head I believe of the Canadian Bankers' Association, before the committee, and when asked if there was sufficient credit to meet the demands of the country he said:
The demand for credit in Canada is less than the banks of Canada are able to take care of, substantially less, and the banks of Canada at the moment have large sums unemployed.
Now in view of the conditions the farmers of western Canada are up against at the present time it is hard to understand that statement.
