When we were asked to subscribe for victory bonds we were all told that those bonds were as good as gold at any time and that they would form a good basis of security if we wanted to borrow. What are the facts? We find that farmers in the West with victory bonds in their possession, who had met with losses in carrying on their farming operations, could not get loans on these bonds and were forced to sell them out and out. In view of that fact it is hard to understand Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor's statement that there is no lack of credit in Canada.
A short time ago I came across this extract from an article by Lord Milner in the London Observer:
Labour is more and more inclined to question the competence of the bigwigs of industry and finance. There is a loss of confidence in the management.
Such loss of confidence may not be wholly justified, but, in view of the extraordinary happenings of the last three or four years, it is not unnatural. Let us try to picture the impression which his experiences during those years are likely to have left on the mind of any fairly intelligent workman, a man, say, good at his own job, but with only so much information about the general affairs of the world as he could gather from the steady perusal of his daily paper. For months and months after the close of the war he had it dinned into his ears that the world was suffering from a shortage of goods, and he was overwhelmed with exhortations to him and the men of his class not to spare themselves, but to work with intensified energy to make up the deficiency. That, he was vehemently assured, was their duty to their country and the world, and at the same time the one sure road to the improvement of their own condition. Such was the unanimous appeal made to him by all the highest authorities in the world of industry and finance. And he obeyed it to the best of his ability, but only to find, a year or two later, that the warehouses of his employers were choked with goods which they could not sell, and that his services were no longer required.

Bank Act
And then, when, stung fey disappointment, he began to probe for himself into the causes of this strange contradiction, he was told that there had unfortunately been a mistake, that the activity to which he had been so fervently exhorted to contribute was "feverish," that he ought to have known, we ought all to have known, that after the war there was bound to be a big slump, because "the pool of capital had been depleted', and we had no money for making things and nobody else had any money for buying them. . .
We all remember very well, when the war was on and afterwards, the advice which was sent out by the financial institutions of this country, especially when we farmers in Canada were complaining about the conditions we have to meet, "We have all got to make our sacrifices, we have all got to be patriotic." I should like to ask the chairman and the members of this committee whether the banks of Canada have taken their share of the losses, whether they have borne their share of the sacrifices undergone by the masses of the people of this country? We found that when the great mass of the people were suffering-not only on the farms but in our cities as well-banks were holding their annual meetings and declaring their usual dividends. At the annual meeting of every bank, while other people were undergoing sacrifices and enduring suffering, it was announced that the year had been a prosperous one and the customary dividends would be paid.
One of the things we hear a great deal of in Canada to-day is the necessity for an aggressive immigration policy. We all realize that we are staggering under a tremendous burden of debt and that in order to develop this vast country we should have more people here. But what inducement can we offer to bring immigrants to Canada? We find that in New Zealand, in Australia, and in the United States they have inaugurated some form of rural credit scheme in order to assist the farmers. We are spending millions of dollars on an immigration policy in order to bring settlers to Canada and what inducement are we offering these settlers? Let me compare what is being done for the farmer in the United States at the present time with what is being done in Canada. If a farmer takes out a loan for $1,000, under the present rural credit scheme, an amortization plan they have over there, in thirty-four years he will have paid back a total of $1,870. The farmer in Canada who takes out a loan of $1,000 must pay interest at the rate of 8 per cent and I may say there are a great many loans that bear a much heavier rate than 8 per cent. Taking out a loan on that basis in thirty-four years, instead of paying back $1,870 as in the case of his American cousin,
he will pay back the much larger sum of $3,700. What inducement, therefore, is there for immigrants to come to Canada when if they settle in this country they have to compete in the same market with people who are much better situated.
I think the hon. member for Halifax admitted, I know many others have admitted, that there was a gap between our present financial system and the farmer. In view of that fact the government would give a great amount of satisfaction, especially to the members on this side, if, instead of trying to force this bill through at the present time, they would await the report of the special committee on agriculture and its recommendation in favour of some rural credit scheme, and give us some assurance that action along that line would be taken. In the absence of such assurance from the government it is our duty to protest that the bill to revise the Bank Act should not be put through at the present time.

Would it not be better to take some of the time now being consumed in trying to develop a rural credit scheme or some financial institution which might meet the situation my hon. friend says prevails to-day in the West? Is there any relation between commercial banking necessarily and a rural credit scheme?

That is what I was trying to tell the hon. gentleman. The special committee on agricultural conditions have spent practically the whole of this session in developing some such scheme, and yet this bill is being forced through in advance of that committee's recommendation.
Now, I do not wish to occupy time unnecessarily. As I said at the beginning of my remarks I did not intend to make any lengthy argument, but I do feel that it is the duty of the government, in view of the existing conditions, to try and evolve some rural credit scheme that will meet the needs of the agriculturists of Canada. One of the things that I know for a fact is this: As a result of the economic conditions that we are now struggling against the farmers are getting into a condition almost of despair, and unless we can take back to those farmers from this long session of parliament some hope-some little ray of hope-that relief is going to be given them to enable them to get out from under the tremendous burden they are carrying, there is going to be a greater exodus from Canada than has been witnessed in the past. I want to give credit to other hon. members in this House. I believe we are all sincerely desirous of building up this country, but I think that after the months we have spent in session
Bank Act

here, this government should try to establish some rural credit scheme that would afford relief to our agriculturists. We find that in practically every other country of the world some scheme of this character has been evolved. To-day the people of Canada are looking to this government for leadership in the matter, and I hope that before this session closes the government will come forward with some scheme calculated to remedy the existing situation.

I rather hesitate to take part in this debate feeling as I do the lack of information which other members in this group possess in relation to the question of bank revision. Before dealing with this subject, I should like to pay my tribute to those members of the Banking committee who have devoted their time so assiduously and who have studied so carefully the different phases of the banking question. I for one, reading only cursorily the reports in the newspapers, have been rather surprised at their astuteness and the careful consideration that has been given to many questions that have come before the Banking committee. I admit that the question has now become rather tedious; it is taking a long time; it has been carefully considered; but I would call the attention of the committee to the fact that a question is never settled until it is settled right, and I question very much if we have reached the place where we can say that this question has been rightly settled.
Perhaps some little trouble was occasioned at the beginning by certain theories being propounded before the Banking committee that rather alarmed some members in the committee and in this House. I might say that they were needlessly alarmed when one takes into consideration who at present occupies the position of Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the composition of this parliament. I think hon. members may rest assured that nothing very radical or serious is likely to happen in this parliament as regards the Bank Act. I have every respect for the Minister of Finance-I will take second place to no one in that regard-but, perhaps, having been in that position for a long time, he ha3 seen things working fairly smoothly; he is certainly well content with things as they are and he is rather careful that, at least, if he should err, he would err upon the side of safety. He has been very safe in this case. From what I can learn, no very great difference has been made in the Bank Act; it is substantially the same Bank Act that we have had during the last ten years.

I believe throughout the country at the present time there is considerable dissatisfaction with our financial conditions, and 1 for one wrould like to see this question carefully considered. I can speak from personal experience. I have in my room upstairs a large volume of evidence that has been taken before the Banking committee. I have not had time to read a single issue of that evidence and I am perfectly certain that, perhaps, the majority of the members of this House are exactly in the same position. They are asked to vote for this Bank Act, and they do not know what all this is about, or what all the evidence is that has been taken before the committee. I do not think in the history of parliament has such a volume of evidence been taken, or has the question been shaken up so thoroughly as during the time evidence has been taken cn the stand before that committee. I claim that as one reason why I think the members of this House and the people of this country should have time to consider this question in all its bearings. I have had requests from bankers to send them some copies of the evidence, and I am sure the bankers of Canada are not acquainted with the evidence, nor have they given it sufficient consideration to enable them to make to their members the suggestions they might make if they were familiar with all that evidence. Perhaps the people who are anxious to go too far have played into the hands of those who do not want to go at all. I do not know if hon. members will understand just what I mean. They have made people afraid, and those who might have been willing to go a little further have been afraid to move just for fear some of the 'ideas that have been propounded should be put into practice. As I said before, this revision will not be final in any case. There should be no antagonism between the different classes in our country. It should be very evident to everyone that banks can live only by the business they do with the people of the country; and if a system is adopted that is detrimental to the business of the country, it does not matter whether that business is agricultural or industrial, in the long run the banks also will suffer, so that the banks and the people after all are interested in seeing that we have a proper financial system.
I have a short extract from an article written by Colonel MacLaren in the last issue of the Financial Post. I will read this, and I want hon. members to pay particular attention. The article reads:
The proceedings before the Bankers' committefe have not improved matters in spite of the efforts of the

Bank Act
chairman, A. K. Maclean, one of the most tactful men in the House, aided by the very broad knowledge of the Minister of Finance. The financiers and the farmers across Canada are drifting into real antagonism.
I for one deplore the fact that there should be any antagonism between the different classes in this Dominion of ours. It should have been the business of the financiers of this country to come forward and give all assistance in their power to provide the very best possible financial institutions. From what I hear-I cannot speak from actual knowledge-the stand taken by the bankers has been that we have an admirable banking system and that it cannot be much improved on. Such an attitude of superiority of great knowledge should not be taken when people know things have not been functioning just as well as they really should. The writer goes on to say:
The blame does not rest with the farmers.
The farmers are not radicals.
I want hon. members to pay attention to that, because I know hon. members in this part of the House are sometimes looked upon as bolshevists and radicals who are willing to upset everything and to create disturbance in every branch and line of industry. Nothing is further from them than that. The writer continues:
They are capitalists themselves, very closely allied to and in deep sympathy with good business and sound finances, and with little real sympathy for political interference in business. They want some sound way of temporary borrowing.
I might go on to say that they want longer credits even than our banks are willing to give at the present time. I should like again to emphasize the statement that farmers as a class are not radicals, nor are they bolshevists. There are no people in this country as able and willing to stand up for the institutions and the welfare of the country as are the farmers of Canada. If you will allow me to make an interjection at this point, I remember the strike in the city of Winnipeg, when the people lost their heads, and the cry heard then was "The farmers will save them; the farmers will save them". Why was that? Because they were the most stable element in the whole population of this Dominion.
There are going to be changes in the coming years in any case. I do not care how this committee votes on the present division; I will make the prophecy,-and I am perfectly sure of it,-that within ten years there are going to be changes in the Bank Act. To my mind, one of the things of greatest importance at the present time in connection with our banking institutions is the matter of credit getting into the hands of a few men. Have
hon. members ever considered what credit means, what power it gives? If ever the credit of Canada gets into the hands of a few men, they can make and unmake industry, institutions, individuals just as they like, and I for one am alarmed to see the banking institutions of our country gradually converging into the hands of a few people. I listened with great attention and pleasure to the very eloquent speech of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey). Like myself he hesitates to discuss currency and banking. They are intricate and rather difficult matters to understand, but I think I know enough to realize that currency and banking are really international affairs and go wider than the bounds of our own Dominion.
I do not intend to make any lengthy speech, for the simple reason that I have given this question no particular study; but I think the members in this part of the House are making a very reasonable request. They are asking nothing out of the way; they are not going to upset any industry. Business can be readily assured that this House is not going to do anything tremendously radical, and business can go on during the years to come, quite confident that nothing is going to happen that will hurt it very much.
Not very much attention has been paid by members on the government side of the House to the fact that we have had requisitions and resolutions passed by governing bodies, two provincial legislatures and a large farming association in the West, asking that the revision be held over for a year, or, at least, that charters be only granted for one year. The senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has said that he has not heard us give any reasons. I think several reasons have been given. One is the fact that we feel the need at the present time of some intermediary system of banking between short-term credits and what may be called the farm loan system of long-term credits. We need some system of rural credit, and as a member once said in the House, we have only one system of banking at present. We have no other. We do not know of any proposition the government is likely to make. I was disappointed when the Minister of Finance made his speech that he did not give some promise that the government was going to look into some system of rural credits for financing the farmers for some three or four years which could be done; and if we allow the Bank Act to go through now, I feel certain that we are not going to see a Dominion system of rural credit for some considerable length of time. I do not wish to
Bank Act

discuss the matter further, because I am not very well posted. I have not had the privilege of attending the meetings and hearing the evidence placed before the committee. I can see nothing unreasonable or out of the way in making the request that the bank charters be extended for one year only. I am sure that members on the other side of the House do not understand public opinion in the West. The statement of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) that the government had received one shot already is perfectly true, and the second shot might be fatal as far as the government is concerned.
Mr. EVANS. There are several reasons why clause 5 should be amended. I think it has been apparent to us now for many years that our Canadian banking system does not adequately meet the needs or the interests throughout this Dominion. I think this is particularly true as regards the basic industry of agriculture. As one of those concerned with that industry, I shall endeavour to give some reasons why the revision of the act should be deferred for another year. A mass of evidence has been secured by the committee on Banking, which, if properly sifted and digested by men capable of dealing with this question would give us a lead by which we could evolve a system which would adequately meet the needs of the basic industry, and serve the needs of the industry of this country in a fair and impartial manner, particularly the basic industry of agriculture which is now mostly suffering. Now, Mr. Chairman, some of those gentlemen who seem so anxious that this revision should take place, have in the recent past given utterance to statements and opinions which would go to show that they themselves realized, to some extent at least, that the present system does not adequately meet the needs of the interests of this Dominion. For instance, Sir Vincent Meredith realized the helplessness of the present system to adequately finance our export trade so as, he said, to keep our factories open and give employment to our workingmen. He said:
If foreign trade can be revived it will solve many of our difficulties.
In fact speaking at the annual meeting of his bank in 1920 he became emphatic and declared that sooner or later this question must be dealt with by the banks, and the fact is, Mr. Chairman, that Sir Vincent Meredith, in this speech to which I now refer, December 6, 1920, realized the helplessness of the banks, to aid the industries and take advantage of any opportunity which fate might offer. So we see that even our bankers are beginning to

realize that our much-lauded Canadian banking system has fallen down in that it fails to meet the immediate needs of the country. It is not merely agriculture that is suffering; in fact it is plain to everyone that our cities to-day are suffering, and that our workingmen have had to migrate to seek work. I think, Sir, it would be a crime to extend the charters for the present inefficient system-yes, admitted to be inefficient-for ten years, without profiting by the experience which has been furnished us by the evidence of those who appeared before the Banking committtee this session. Theoretically, our system is as efficient as it was twenty years ago when we had money to assist in the harvesting of the United States crop, according to William Long Baker, who has written a very able treatise on banking in Canada. But, I think the most interesting point of this candid confession of weakness is that, in so far as the public is concerned, no move has been made to cure the trouble. Two whole years have gone by since Sir Vincent Meredith recognized this, and our bankers who have realized their own weakness have done nothing to improve the trade of the country, and the responsibility for that certainly rests on the shoulders of such a body of men, seeing that it is they who control the circulation of the very lifeblood of industry-finance. Our factories have not been busy, and were it not for our close proximity to the United States we would, this last winter, have had an unemployment problem on our hands such as we never saw before, and indeed, it is questionable if our Acting Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) would have been able to cope with the awful disturbances that would surely have ensued.
All these conditions exist in Canada, while an unprecedented era of peace and industry prevail in the United States under a more elastic system of credit. But agriculture is not the only industry that has fallen down. If the capitalistic system of our country is all right, why are not our industries working? Now, while a patriotic minority in this House seeks to put off the revision of our banking system for another year, we find the present banking combine able to control parliament to such an extent that the representatives of the people jealously guard the present inadequate and contracting system at the expense of industry. The banks are semi-public institutions. They are joint stock companies founded for private gain, but they accomplish this end with the earnings of the public. A question which should be answered to-day is: What are our seventeen bankers doing in the public interest? It is time, in the interests of this country, that this awful monopoly con-

Bank Act
trolling industry and credit should be broken, and this House will commit a crime against the workers of the land if they renew the present system with only such minor amendments as are contemplated in the amended draft before us.
The banking system is a monopoly and has been for years until to-day it is able to entirely control industry in any way it chooses. Under this system the public have no voice in the direction in which their earnings are loaned. Taking September 30th last, the total paid-up capital of the seventeen chartered banks I find to be $125,004,717; the total liabilities $2,342,980,663; the deposits amounted to the tremendous sum of $1,648,647,555. So we see to what extent the banks are indebted to the public for the deposits on which they make so large a part of their profits. We also see to what extent the people have trusted the banks until they have become such a complete monopoly that they are bound by no law whatsoever. They take the people's deposits at 3 per cent and loan them out for anything up to 9 or 10 per cent. All renewed loans this year in the West, so far as I can find out, are made at 9 per cent, unless interest is paid in advance. In a letter from an old friend in my constituency who lives adjacent to the town of Asquith he has this to say:
I told you they had increased the rate from 8 to 9 per cent. This time I wanted to know what the rate was, and was told I could have the note renewed at 8 per cent. When the note was being made out I was asked if I intended paying the interest then. I asked why. Why should I pay interest for a period of service before the service began? He replied that I could pay at the end if I like, but it would be some more, and altered the note accordingly to 9 per cent.
And he asks:
Is it not time the paying interest beforehand, or alternately paying interest on interest, for which no service has been given was changed? Why not have a straight rate to be charged after the service has been given? The present system seems only useful to confound the average customer until we don't know exactly what we are paying.
I submit, Sir, that as things are at present the farmers cannot pay 8 or 9 per cent. I think a commission of inquiry between now and next session could do splendid work in establishing these facts, and then we could deal with the revision in an intelligent manner.
Our banking monopoly is given privileges not equalled in any other country in the world. The banks may, without making any deposits in the central gold reserve, issue notes up to the full amount of their unimpaired capital, and it is incorrect indeed to suppose, as we did in the past, that the whole of the bank notes in circulation are backed by deposits of gold. It is not so. This is a very valuable privilege, and it enables our banks to open branches throughout the whole country. They say they do this to serve the needs of the people. I am not so sure of that. Sir Edmund Walker, giving evidence before the Banking committee in 1913, admitted that it was the profits from the note issue that permitted the banks to open such a large number of branches. At present I think the seventeen chartered banks have about four thousand branches throughout the country. It is time that this privilege was curtailed and some check placed upon this free issue.
I know the banks are required to make monthly returns. The Minister of Finance, too, may call for special returns at any time. But what value we may attach to these returns in the face of what transpired in the Merchants Bank failure, when the president and other officials were exonerated from all blame, is more than I know. It is hardly to be expected that a concern of this kind would let the public know its exact condition, par-ticlarly if it happened to be on the down grade.
I think one of the chief reasons why this revision should be delayed, or granted only for one year, is the fact that our banking monopoly has the power in its hands to enhance the price of any commodity and, on the other hand, to cripple any industry by withholding credit. This is certainly a power that should not be given into the hands of any class of men. The branch banks exist for collecting the people's earnings, to be used in any other part of the country instead of for the development of the community in which those earnings were made. Now, Mr. Chairman, the trouble with different parts of our country to-day is that the branch bank system collects the earnings of the people to be used in enterprises far remote from where those earnings have been gathered, and I submit that the West in particular is suffering from this evil to-day. We have no industries in western Canada, nor are we likely to have as long as our earnings are tapped for the benefit of industries in other parts of the country. Indeed, there is only one banking concern that has its headquarters west of the Great Lakes. I say it is a real objection to our banking system as at present constituted and carried on that no profits, or practically none, are distributed in the locality where they are made. The whole monopoly is used for the benefit of the monopoly and is more and more impoverishing the rural parts of the Dominion. Indeed, Sir, it is to be regretted that to this accursed system of centralization of
Bank Act

capital and industry the Dominion to-day stands indebted for a contracted population of eight or nine million people instead of more than double that number, as we should have.
I have said that the banks are a law unto themselves. In the West they have always charged what interest they chose to exact, and they have always compelled the payment of notes at any time they pleased to name. Indeed, it is not so long ago, in 1907 in fact, when the banks took part in a great conspiracy to compel the western grain grower to ship his grain through the Grain Combine's elevator instead of using the loading platform. I think the banks went outside their proper sphere of business in taking that action. I think they should be prevented from purchas-ng agricultural products, particularly for speculative purposes. I do not think it is a healthy state of affairs for any people when they are at the mercy of a combine or of combines who dictate the methods they shall use to market their products. No one can estimate the possibilities of Canada's future. No one knows far ahead what problems we may have to solve. Our financial system is the pivot on which everything else revolves, and it is surely in the public interest that this revision should be put off until the people in the country can make their wants known along lines of experience as brought out before the Banking committee of the present session.

Mr. Chairman, I want to protest against this shoving of the Bank Act through and the granting of the charters for another ten years-which is speaking in favour of the amendment. I believe that the charters should be granted for one year only. I have not prepared a speech, but I do not feel that I should let this opportunity pass without adding my voice to the volume of voices that has arisen in protest against the undue haste of the bankers and their friends in this matter. Our request is surely a very reasonable one, and it has that which is necessary in parliament to give it an air of respectability; it has a precedent. Now, I was a member of the Banking committee

not an able one, I am willing to admit that, but at least an interested one and one who attended the meetings quite regularly. I found that it was generally the bankers who came there to give evidence; that the small manufacturer-in fact, the large one-the businessman, the representatives of basic industries, did not come to give their evidence and to tell how the Bank Act as at present constituted affected their business. To me 
this is a very good reason why the final revision of the Bank Act should be postponed and the charters granted for one year only. The attitude of members of the Banking committee and the harmony with which the two old traditional parties worked together there brought me to the position where I felt it would be well to grant the charters for one year only instead of for ten.
Now, the question of national currency is a very large one. A great many people today think we should have a national currency instead of the bank currency; others think that either the bankers or the government should go into the issuing of currency, but not both. Then, there are a great many who think that this privilege of issuing currency is a valuable one for which the banks do not pay sufficiently either in the form of taxes to the government or in the form of services to the public. That would seem to me a very good reason for asking that the revision be postponed for one year. In talking to manufacturers-not only to a few, but to many-I found that all honest manufacturers objected most strenuously to section 88 and were very anxious that it should be changed. They should be given a hearing, surely; they are usually given a hearing by the government of Canada, I think, and I do not see why they should be discriminated against in this particular instance. On the other hand, from the banks' point of view, they claim that the Bank Act is perfect. Well, if it is, it will stand being looked at for another year -because perfection will bear scrutiny. Indeed, if the Bank Act is perfect, the bankers, their eminent counsel, the government and their friends in the opposition, would gain by allowing the public to have a good look at it, because it would strengthen their position; it would show that we who are attacking it are wrong, and you would then have the club over our head. So from your own point of view, since you people who know so much about it are sure it is perfect, it would be well for you to let us have a look at it; it would, according to your argument, simply strengthen your own position.
It seems to me an odd thing for a Liberal government that stands for a fuller life and larger freedom-or is it a larger life and fuller freedom-to insist on rushing the Bank Act through this year. I am going to give you a little warning. I am not anxious to save the government, and never have been, as my course in this House has proved. But I am going to tell you this: You may unite with the official opposition; you may work with what I am quite convinced is great pressure from behind, but if in opposition to the just

Bank Act
demands of legitimate industry, not only farming but other basic industries, and not only basic industries, but the key industries that are usually called the secondary industries-if in opposition to these you insist on forcing it through, you are only bringing destruction on yourself. It is written, I believe, that "whom the gods would destroy they first make mad;" so it is your affair-and it will be your funeral, not ours. You see, the very fact that you people who stand for rushing it through are so anxious to do that makes the general public suspicious that there is some particular reason for the hurry.
Of course, bankers have ever been moral cowards; they have always been afraid. When two leading banks in England many years ago decided to give out bank books and allow people to issue cheques against their deposits, the other banks said it would be the ruination of the financial system, but as everybody knows the financial system is standing strong and steady yet. You remember what Professor Fisher of Yale University said-and we cannot discount all his statements-that bankers were natural standpatters; that they were afraid of change. Some of the people who know these bankers well ought to tell them to buck up and not be so utterly frightened; they would gain more by not being so fearful about these things. I was in the country for four days and I talked Bank Act everywhere I went. I asked everybody I talked to privately what they thought about it [DOT]-business people, manufacturers, farmers, professional men-and I met none who said they thought the Bank Act should go through this year. They were of the opinion that it had been too long a session-whether a fruitful one, at least a wearisome one; that something had to be discarded unless we were to stay here a great length of time yet; that it was reasonable to leave the Bank Act over, particularly in view of the fact that the evidence had not been considered, that it was a rushed affair.
I said, too, when this matter came up in committee, and I would like to say it again: If the rush was so great, why did the government not start sooner? It is a wonder it was left until after Easter if the rush was so great. I was willing to have come here much earlier; I was willing to have sat in committee long before Easter, and I think a great many other members were too. This hurry, I say, does seem odd, and I know it seems odd to a great many others. A large number of the people think the banking system as at present constituted does not serve productive industry; that it much more generously serves speculation. If once that idea gets fastened in the public mind it will be a
very disastrous thing for the banks and for the friends of the bankers. So, I say, why not be reasonable while you have yet the chance? At least if you are unreasonable, and if some years from now you wish you had not been, remember that I warned you.

I rise to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), and I hope that I shall be able to give at least one reason that will be considered to be such by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). Of course, the debate has advanced considerably since that hon. gentleman made the remark that no reason had been offered why the bank charters should be extended for one year only instead of ten. It is difficult for me to decide what would constitute a reason for the hon. member for Halifax, for we all reason somewhat differently. I am sorry, however, that while he did not consider as arguments what were put forward as such by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, he did not do them the courtesy of even considering their utterances as arguments at 'least from their own point of view and answering them accordingly. However, he chose to sweep them aside with a mystic wave of the hand and say, they are not arguments at ail. That is the easiest way I know out of a difficulty on the floor of this House or anywhere else in debate, simply to say that what the opponent has said is not an argument and leave it at that.
Another thing that the hon. member for Halifax said was that he did not know how long it was going to take hon. members over on this side of the House to make up their minds. Were they going to take all day, a week, a month or a decade to make up their minds, was his query? Well, I cannot speak for the Progressives in that regard. I do not know how long they are going to take to make up their minds on this question, but I would say to the committee that it would be better for us to take ten years to make up our mind and make it up right than to pass an inadequate act that will last ten years, an act that has no mind in it at all. That would be a better proposition. I would suggest, however, that it did not take the hon. member for Halifax very long to make up his mind on this matter. He did it with great haste seemingly. In fact, I think he was always ready to pass the act even before we began to consider it, judging from his attitude in committee.
I was surprised, however, when the hon. member for Halifax confessed to knowing about the Merchants Bank collapse. It has been advanced by hon. members on this side
Bank Act

of the House that an investigation should be held into the Merchants Bank failure. The reason they are asking for that is that one of the functions of the Bank Act, or at least of the act as it should have been revised, would be to prohibit any such recurrence as the collapse of the Merchants Bank, but we cannot make an act that will safeguard against a recurrence of the Merchants Bank incident unless we know why it was that the Merchants Bank failed. When we were in committee, Mr. Chairman, nobody knew why the Merchants Bank failed. The hon. member for Halifax did not know why the Merchants Bank failed. The Finance Minister declared that he did not know. Sir Edmund Walker declared that he did not know. Nobody knew in committee why the Merchants Bank failed, but now the hon. member for Halifax knows. In fact, he comes in with a huge blanket, a blanket that is broad enough and long enough to cover up every crime in history, and he places that right over the Merchants Bank condition and says that it was due to human frailty. He goes further than that. After he has told us why it failed, he proves to us that it did not fail at all. That is good reasoning. He says it only weakened a little in the joints, so to speak, and when it got wobbly it fell gently into the arms of a larger institution. Now it might be necessary for us to find out just how the arms of the other institution came to be there to receive the Merchants Bank when it got wobbly in the joints. That might be a good reason why the revision of the Bank Act should be postponed for another year. If the Merchants Bank did not fail, did not something worse happen to it than that, something far more dangerous to the people of Canada than even a bank failure?
Will the hon. gentleman permit me to tell him that the Merchants Bank did not fail?

I thank the hon. gentleman for restating what I had just stated, that the opinion of the hon. member for Halifax, which I think in this regard ought to be a good one, is that the Merchants Bank did not fail, it only weakened. I am saying that if it did not fail it constitutes a more dangerous situation for the people of Canada and for the industries of this country than if it did fail, because it suggests a condition which permits a fuller development of banking mergers in this country. The banking merger is growing apace. We are reduced now, I think, to seventeen banks-seventeen banks with one single

voice. They meet together in association, they fix the rate of interest on deposits, they fix the rate of interest on loans-a huge co-operative monopoly. If, I repeat, the Merchants Bank did not fail, if it was swallowed by a larger institution of the same kind, that is a menace far more to be feared than the mere failure of the bank would have constituted.
Now, I cannot speak about the Merchants Bank failure because I do not know why it happened, or if it was not a failure, I do not know what it was. All that I know is this, that the Merchants Bank, which was one of the largest banking institutions in this country, suddenly stopped doing business as the Merchants Bank, and as a result of the stoppage some $5,500,000 of the shareholders' money was lost and the whole Institution passed into the hands of the Bank of Montreal at a very, very low price indeed. It is true I believe that when the Bank of Montreal took over the Merchants Bank, the Merchants Bank had some one and a half million dollars still in reserve, and I also believe that it was considered to be in a solvent condition. If so, how did it come that the Bank of Montreal got such an excellent deal in taking it over? That is another thing that ought to be explained. Perhaps it would be wise to have an investigation into that alone. That is a matter of interest to the Canadian people; it is of interest to the shareholders of that bank; it is of interest to the shareholders of all banks because the same thing may be repeated in connection with another bank next year. That in itself in my opinion, Mr. Chairman, constitutes an argument why this act should not now be passed extending these charters for ten years. If it is not an argument I would like the hon. member for Halifax to tell me what is the weakness about it. What is the matter with the argument? I would like him to tell me and answer it.

I have no hesitation in telling my hon. friend that it is no argument at all. Perhaps he might inform the House by telling us what relation there is between the failure of the Merchants Bank, or the losses it sustained which later induced it to sell out to another bank, and the present act which we are considering. Can my hon. friend inform the House of that?

I am glad, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member has pointed out to me that I have failed to make myself clear to him. I shall now take the opportunity of restating very briefly the relation between the

Bank Act
present act and the failure or non-failure of the Merchants Bank.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has been discussing the case of the Merchants Bank, he must confine himself to clause 5 of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, I quite understand that. What I am discussing is the amendment to clause 5 and that amendment asks for the renewal of the bank charters for one year instead of renewing them for ten years, and I am trying to make an argument why the renewal should only be for one year instead of ten. At the same time I am answering a question bearing upon the particular point. I am going to advance the argument that the failure of the Merchants Bank has a direct connection with this bill and with this particular clause, and I shall do it in this way: As a result of the trial which took place over the Merchants Bank nobody was punished. I presume they were not punished because it was discovered that they had not violated any clause of the Bank Act. If what happened in the Merchants Bank case transpired without violating any clause of the Bank Act then it is clear that there was nothing in that act which prevented such an occurrence from taking place. My argument then is, that seeing we are now revising the Bank Act we should have a clause or clauses which would make it impossible for that kind of thing to take place and for people who commit such malpractice to stay out of gaol.
The next step in the argument is this: It is the duty of this parliament to amend the Bank Act in such a way as to make the Merchants Bank case impossible of recurrence. We cannot do that unless we know what happened in the Merchants Bank case. We cannot know what happened there unless we investigate it, and we cannot investigate it unless the bill be referred back to committee or unless we have an opportunity which an extension for another year would give us. If we pass this bill and let the matter go for ten years, and if in the meantime two or three other banks fail in a similar manner- in such an event what argument then will the hon. member for Halifax bring forward when we confront him with the opportunity which is afforded now of amending this in a way that would render it impossible for such a thing to occur without those affected being able at least to put their hands on the guilty parties? That is the argument which connects the Merchants Bank case directly with this bill and with the particular clause under discussion.
Now, as I was saying when the hon. member interrupted me, the Merchants Bank was seemingly in a solvent condition when it waa taken over. One of two things seems to be certain so far as I have been able to gather from the evidence that was brought out during the trial, as well as from questions which were put in committee. Either there was very bad management which might have been safeguarded by legislation, and was not, which accounted for the position of the Merchants Bank, or else there was a frame-up for a merger from which frame-up the Bank of Montreal profited. Now, there are the only two possible solutions of the difficulty that I can conceive, and I do not think it is fair that the people of Canada should be left in doubt as to which of these two things was the correct reason. Again I say the only way to settle that is by an investigation, and the only way to get an investigation is to pass this amendment and to grant the charters for one year, then take the bill up again next year and revise it and pass it for ten years if desired. That is the argument. The cause is not known. We have, as I pointed out, two probable causes and I have given them to you. We have, in addition to the two probable causes with regard to the Merchants Bank case, one anticipation and one certainty. The anticipation is that under the present Bank Act some other bank might come into the same difficulty as we found in the case of the Merchants Bank. The certainty, the only certainty we have in regard to the whole affair is that the confidence of the people of Canada has been shaken in the banking system. It is all very well for the hon. member for Halifax to stand up and say, with a smile of complacency and virtue," We have the greatest banking system in the world," but when we have a banking system which allows such a thing as happened in the Merchants Bank case, we have an argument that is far more potent in the public mind that the mere statement of even such a gentleman as my hon. friend.
May I ask my hon. friend not to state that I said it was the best banking system in the world because the hon. gentleman must know I did not say that.	[DOT]
If I misquoted the hon. gentleman I must apologize but I understood him to say that. If he did not say it was the best system in the world I would like him to tell me just how good it is.

I would rather my hon. friend devote his time to showing why we should postpone this bill; he has not started on it yet.
Bank Act

As I pointed out at the
outset, as to what constitutes an argument depends as much upon the mentality of those who listen as upon the mentality of the man who is making the argument. With that remark I shall leave my argument to the judgment of the House and to the judgment of those who may some time enter the sarcophagus in which we are now to bury this argument and look at what is said on this issue.

Before the hon. gentleman quits that part of his argument will he tell me whether he is prepared to state that if this delay is granted he will be able to frame an act which will prevent any bank getting into trouble in the future?

That question, Mr. Chairman is unworthy of the brilliance that I know the hon. member who asked the question possesses. I am not called upon to make any prophecy as to what might be the possible outcome of the investigation. True we might investigate and discover nothing but even if we did that it would be a certain amount of satisfaction. Then we might investigate and find out something wrong and not be able to rectify it, in which case our plight would amount to a defeat of the intelligence of this parliament. But to expect me to make now a definite promise that I will frame an act which will meet any difficulty we may encounter in the investigation requested is asking something that I think is altogether unreasonable.
Now, let me proceed with another argument and I do hope that the hon. member for Halifax will see there is reason in this. Just before doing so I want to go back for a minute to the statement which has been made, I think in the Banking and Commerce committee if it has not been made in Committee of the Whole, that the Bank Act as it is now is not a fixed thing, that it may be changed once a year if we so desire it. That is a very plausible argument and I want to deal
11 p.m. with it for a moment before I advance another reason why this bill should be postponed as we require. It seems to be democratic, it seems to be theoretically right, when we say that this act is not fixed at all, that it may be amended any day, that parliament is supreme in this matter. That sounds good but if we just puncture that bubble there is nothing left of it. Let us see how we would begin to puncture it. In the first place there is a moral obligation involved in this franchise, a moral obligation which I do not hesitate to say would be very speedily advanced on the part of hon. gentlemen oppo-

site if we were to bring in next year a clause to amend some fundamental principle in the Bank Act. But leaving that aside, how is it going to be amended, who is going to do it? I do not see the government doing it; I have no vision of that at all. If there was going tc be any amendment whatsoever in this Bank Act next year, or the year following, or any year within the decade we are allotting it, such amendment would have to be brought in by some private member. What opportunity has a private member to get a bill through this House? He has an excellent opportunity theoretically. Why, if I were over in the United States and boasting of the fine parliamentary system we have in this country I could say in my speech that I could pass any act. But as a private member in this House, I cannot even get one before the House. I brought in a private bill this year, the first one I think on the order paper. It is still there, and it will be there next year and I have no assurance that next year will be more favourable. Again let us not forget that there is always the opportunity of ruling it out of order because it involves a public expenditure. We cannot pass a private bill without printing it on paper, and if we print it on paper, that involves a public expenditure. If public expenditure is involved, then no private member can bring in a bill. Who is going to amend the Bank Act?
The Bank Act was amended three times between 1913 and this year.

If the Bank Act was
amended three times, I would not be surprised if the amendments came as a suggestion from the bankers, were carried out by the government of the day and did not constitute a fundamental amendment. I think you will find Sir Edmund Walker congratulating himself and the Bankers' Association on the fact that any amendment that has ever been made to the Bank Act has been the direct suggestion of the Bankers' Association. That, to my mind, does not constitute an amendment of the character I am speaking in favour of now. I have no doubt amendments will be made, if they are in the interests of the bankers; but if they are in the interests of a new financial system, they will not be introduced, they will not be made.
Let me come to another reason, and, I think, even a more important reason why the charters should be granted for one year only than that of the investigation of the Merchants Bank case. I propose to show that, at this time the charters should not be extended for ten years by this parliament to the banks of Canada, because there must be.

I believe, a readjustment of the financial system to meet modern industrial conditions if a serious disaster is to be prevented in the near future. In support of that contention, let me say to the committee that at the present time our ideas, the ideas of the civilized world, are not moving as fast as events are moving. Events are moving much faster than we are thinking. If the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) will assure me that he is thinking in finance ten years ahead of the industrial situation, I would pass this bill with at least, a greater measure of confidence. But 1 doubt that very much; I doubt whether any of us are capable of thinking ten years ahead. In the face of the swiftness of the changing industrial panorama of the present time, we cannot think that far ahead. If we fix the Bank Act now, and five years from now changes come which might practically tie up the whole industrial system, what are you going to do? Would it not be better for us to consider this carefully as we go, to take into consideration as far as we possibly can all the factors before we fix an act for ten years? Will the present financial system last ten years? Will the government assure the committee that it will? If the government knows that the system is going to last ten years will they inform the House as to the ground for their faith; what are the reasons that this act must be passed this year? What are the reasons the government can give to assure us that the financial system will last for ten years more. It will take more than the Bank Act to stop the financial system	from falling.	The	Bank Act
is not an act which will support the financial system; it is an act which will support the bankers. It will hold up the bankers as long as the system stands, but it will not hold up the system. The system is greater than even the Bank Act and greater than even the government is. The life of the system depends, not upon the Bank Act, but upon economic conditions.
In support of my contention that in ten years some very serious problems will arise involving fundamental changes, I wish to say first that there are at least, two ominous signs that there will be great need of change before ten years are up. Let me refer in the first place in this connection to the great industrial paradox which ought to challenge the thought of all thinking people. The paradox is this: On the one hand we have a superabundance of raw material, of plant equipment and of labour, sufficient by all calculation to bring into being all the goods civilization requires for its necessities. On the other hand, we have communities in dire need of
those very commodities we have the potentiality to produce. That is the industrial paradox, and the financial system, as I shall show, has a very close and direct connection with that industrial paradox. The situation is growing worse; it is growing serious, and before ten years go by a condition may develop which will compel, on the part of those in command of affairs, speedy action which may afterwards be regretted if it is not taken after serious and careful consideration. But there are other examples of this kind. Let me give the committee a sample. Nearly all the victorious countries in the last great war. for instance, claimed that Germany should be compelled to pay; but they discovered that the more Germany paid, the worse it was for the recipients. There is another paradox. There was a time when our financial system was at such a stage of development that it was possible for one nation to pay another without making the nation that received worse off than it was before. But the industrial situation has developed to such an extent that the more Germany pays Great Britain, for instance, the worse it becomes for Great Britain. That is a fact that we have to face. What does that mean? It means that the events in the industrial world have changed much faster than the financial ideas of financiers, changed so fast that the financier is defeated in his own purpose. That is an argument, I submit, in favour of our taking time and going slowly with the revision of the Bank Act, because in ten years more serious developments may have taken place, and the financial system may utterly collapse beneath the industrial demands.
The second sign of this decay is in what I am going to call the impotence of govem-meqts and of industrial masters to deal with the developing situation. If there were in the action of the present government any assurance that it was capable of handling a situation such as I have hinted might develop, if there were any assurances given that the actions of the government would be such as to guarantee the continuation of the industrial system producing goods for human needs, no matter what might take place, I would support this bill with much less reluctance. But let me summarize the advice of governments generally and the advice of leaders in the industrial world with respect to the problem which I have just suggested to the committee. First of all, I think nearly every government, certainly our present government in Canada, consoles itself with the idea that the present industrial situation is one that grew out of the war; that similar occurrences have followed war throughout history.
Bank Act

in short that depression is the inevitable result of war. It advises the people of this country to grin and bear it. Just keep on grinning and bearing it. It will come out all right in the end somehow; we do not know just how but it is coming. I submit it is going; it is not coming at all. That is merely a more or less blind consolation. I think nearly all governments have followed that example in taking consolation to themselves from the platitudes of the centuiies past, but the platitudes of the centuries past have proved themselves entirely incapable of meeting immediate practical problems. Then the next consolation which we get from our government is that it is not so bad in this country as it is in other countries. That is the next step the present government takes, and that is what other governments say to the people who are troubled about having no work to do, or about their inability to meet the financial situation, or the tremendous percentages of bankruptcies that have occurred. They say, "We are told these things are not so bad here as they are in other countries". When you come to Great Britain they say the same thing. In the United States they say the same thing, and in Germany the same thing is repeated. I would like to know who is right in that case, but it is poor consolation and poor argument after all. It is like a man standing on the street watching a block of houses burning. His house is one of the block, and all the rest of the houses are blazing, but he turns to the man next to him and says, "Never mind, my house is not blazing nearly as badly as yours, and the situation is not so bad for me as it is for you". That would be poor consolation for a man, and so it is poor consolation for the people of this country, or the people of any other country to be told that the people of other countries are in just as bad a condition. Then the government take another step and they say "Produce more; the only solution for the present situation is more production, grow more wheat and more everything, and manufacture more, and that will help matters". But, unfortunately that advice was taken in this country after the war, and it resulted in adding to the large amount of unsaleable goods on hand, and when that great addition came in the increased production, the wheels of industry stopped and the unemployed masses walked the streets and threateningly challenged the whole basis of civilized order. The next advice which they had to give us is that we consume less.

I certainly do not want to appear as not speaking to the matter under discussion, but I feel certain in my own mind that I am in order, and if the Chairman will bear with me, I would like to show him the purpose for which I wish to use the argument. I am contending that the industrial condition that is developing before our very eyes is so serious that before another ten years it may threaten the civilized world, that it has a very close connection to finance, that if we pass a Bank Act determining the disposition of money and credit for ten years, the industrial crisis that is brewing may come upon us. I am advancing arguments to show further that the government so far is not aware of the situation and I am offering their own words and opinions as proof that they do not know, I contend that my argument bears directly upon the clause of the bill before the committee. But still, as I develop the point, Mr. Chairman, if you decide it otherwise, just tell me so, and I shall have to abide by your ruling. When the government in power tells the masses of the people that the only solution of the problem is to consume less, then they find that if less is consumed, more goods are left on hand which are unsaleable. Moreover, they find it is difficult to invite people who have not enough to consume now, to consume less. So they abandon that position. Then again they say, "We will fix the situation for the farmer in Canada, not by the Bank Act, but by giving him a foreign market." That is what other governments say. All governments try to console the people by saying that somewhere they are going to find a foreign market which will stimulate trade in the particular country concerned. This foreign market promise does not merely mean the exchange of goods for other goods, but it means that we shall ultimately build up a favourable balance of trade with other nations.
