speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to section 5 of rule 13, which says:
Speeches in committee of the whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
On that clause, I rule that the line of discussion pursued by the hon. member is not strictly relevant to the item under discussion.

On the point of order, it seems to me that in considering the question of whether or not the charters of the banks should be granted for one year or ten years, practically unlimited latitude is necessarily involved. I would very respectfully submit that, in considering a matter of this sort, the widest possible light that can be thrown on any aspect of the financial situation is entirely relevant.
Would the hon. gentleman from Brant say whether the hon. member for Calgary East should be permitted to talk for one year or for ten years on this question?

If the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) wishes to limit the hon. member for Calgary East to any specific time, then I would ask him to introduce his closure, but until he does that the hon. member for Calgary East is going to take advantage of the privileges which are offered to hon. members of this House. I am prepared to abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but, perhaps, if I sum up the point I have been leading up to even the Chairman will admit that it is entirely relevant. Here is the summing up. Under the present industrial situation there is not enough being consumed to keep the wheels of production going round. That has transpired, because there is not sufficient purchasing power to enable the people to get all they want to consume. There is not sufficient purchasing power, because we have had a Bank Act in force for ten years, which placed the matter of public credit in the hands of a few individuals. There is the point at issue, and if the Chairman had permitted me I should have marshalled the argument so as to make that connection; but since I am ruled out of order, I leave the conclusion to the committee, and will allow members to use their imagination in developing the argument for themselves. Then, before another ten years, the conflict between science and the money system on the industrial field may possibly have come to a head. Here is the argument. There is a conflict between science as applied to production and the financial system which
should function as the distributing agent of what is produced to the consumer. If we pass an act now which fixes for ten years the financial system of Canada, or the handling of the financial system of Canada, and if during that ten years this conflict between science and the financial system should come to a head, then we are due for a collapse, and for that reason I urge that we pass this act for only one year, that we extend the charter for only one year, and that subsequently we prepare, in the light of the industrial conditions that are threatening civilization, a banking act with a view to meeting these conditions, adequately.
Apropos of that point, let me say that the conflict I have mentioned is simply that in the industrial world to-day we have two great factors which tend to displace human agency. The first is the invention of new machines, and we have the application of science in the harnessing of solar or atomic energy. These two factors, combined and applied to the producing system, take the place of human agency. Now, Mr. Chairman, before you rule me out of order, let me show the connection. When solar energy is applied to machinery, or when machines are improved, less human labour is required, and when less labour is required less money will be paid in wages. The money paid out in wages or dividends under the producing system is the extent of the purchasing power of a nation, and the more machinery is applied to the producing system the more human labour is displaced, the less wages will be paid, and therefore the less money will be in circulation. The less purchasing power the nation has in proportion to what is produced, the greater will be unemployment, the more acute will be the industrial problem. For this reason we would not be wise to pass a Bank Act to remain in force for ten years in the face of these developing conditions, so fraught with serious consequences for all the peoples of the world.
Carried.

I have no doubt that hon. members opposite are very anxious to carry this measure, but I am not in such a hurry. I am quite prepared to consider the bill before we carry it. Simply because hon. members opposite do not need to give the subject consideration is not an argument for this side of the House failing to see their duty to consider the bill very carefully.
I have one more point to make, Mr. Chairman. It has been referred to already. The evidence taken before the committee on

Bank Act

Banking and Commerce in relation to the bill under discussion has not been considered by that committee. I presumed that that evidence was taken with a view to amending the Bank Act, but I discover now that it was taken merely as a gesture, seemingly to appease the public. But let me assure the public that whether the evidence was of value or not has had no effect whatsoever upon the revision of the Bank Act, indeed, it has not been considered at all in that connection. Now, from that point of view I cannot see why the proceedings should be called a revision of the Bank Act, there has been no revision. The act might just as well have been read over casually and passed. If the evidence taken is to give value for the money expended in taking it, it must at least be considered. If it is going to be considered, it ought to be considered before the act is revised for another ten years. So without belabouring that point overmuch, Mr. Chairman, I urge that as an argument why this act should not be now passed for another ten years.
For the benefit again of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), let me point out to him the three reasons which I have attempted to bring forward why the charters should be granted for one year only. In the first place, I have shown that until the facts are known we cannot amend this act to intelligently meet the weaknesses which must have been inherent in it when the Merchants Bank could be wrecked without anyone being found responsible. We must know what was the cause of that failure; the only way to know is to investigate the circumstances, and the only way to investigate the circumstances is to put this revision off until next year. My second point is that industrial conditions, not only in Canada but universally, are developing with such rapidity that old financial ideas are absolutely incapable of handling the situation, that if we fix our banking system now for another ten years in the face of the speedy change that is taking place before our eyes, we are inviting financial and industrial catastrophe. We ought at least to be in a position to keep an open mind on the question as the changes take place, and be prepared to meet them. In the third place, the Bank Act has not been in any way affected by the weight of evidence which was presented to the committee, that if there was any reason for collecting the evidence concurrently with the revision of the act that reason was presumably that it might in some way affect the wording or change the act. But it could not possibly affect the act in any way if not con-

sidered. Therefore I urge that it should be considered before this act is disposed of for ten years.
These are the three reasons I have presented, Mr. Chairman. I could give three more-and I probably will after I have had a rest-but I submit now that these three reasons have to be answered by the hon. member for Halifax or some other worthy representative from the other side before it is necessary for me to advance any further argument. In my estimation what I have urged is sufficient for the carrying of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman).

Mr. Chairman, in the course of the remarks made by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine) I had occasion to interrupt and draw his attention to the fact that the Bank Act has been amended on several occasions and in very important particulars between the revision in 1913 and the present day. The hon. gentleman, with that manner which is characteristic of him, brushed my interruption aside with a so-called or alleged joke. He stated that if the act was amended as I claimed it had been, it must have been done at the behest of the Bankers' Association and by the government, which I gathered from his remarks was considered merely a weak instrument in the hands of the Bankers' Association. Now, I should have thought that after fifty sessions, during which this Banking committee functioned-fifty sessions, at most of which the hon. gentleman was heard with great effect-he might have learned something about the Bank Act. But I find that he has not even read the act. In that respect he reminds me of the story of a famous reviewer of books, who said he never read a book before he reviewed it, because if he did it would prejudice him. Now, I would ask the hon. gentleman what he thinks of these amendments which were passed after 1913, the date of the last revision.
Do you ask a question now?
No, I am making a statement.
Because I might answer it.

Take the amendment passed in 1915, two years after the revision:
The hank may lend money to the owner, tenant, or occupier of land for the purchase of seed grain upon the security of any crop to be grown from such seed grain.
I should like to know in what respect the Bankers' Association only were benefited by that amendment. Again I would refer him to

Bank Act
the amending act of 1916, in which it is stated:
The bank may lend money to a farmer or to any person engaged in stock raising upon the security of his live stock.
I would imagine that these amendments were for the benefit of the party of which he is presumed to be the leader, or one of the leaders. The hon. gentleman, in his very voluble remarks to-night, as on all occasions, reminds me of a cuttlefish. The cuttlefish is a kind of fish which when closely pursued emits a murky fluid from its body, and when the water is thoroughly darkened it escapes. That is the position in which my hon. friend finds himself to-night. Now, I suggest that when he presumes to talk upon the Bank Act-
What is the connection between my hon. friend's remarks and the point under discussion?

The hon. gentleman talks
upon the subject of the Bank Act with the same facility with which he talks on every other question which comes before this House -volubly and at great length. But, as he himself put it somewhat pointedly, when you puncture the bubble, you find there is not very much in it.
Now, the hon. gentleman gives three alleged reasons why this Bank Act should not be proceeded with this year. He spoke about the Merchants Bank and the trouble into which that institution got some time ago- he spoke about it as a failure. Well, I am not going to bandy words with him, but I would like to know what the Merchants Bank, or the failure, if he likes to call it that, has to do with the revision of the Bank Act. After all, the Merchants Bank trouble arose through what was claimed by the department to be failure on the part of the manager to make proper returns as provided in the act. That is all found within one clause of the Bank Act; why hold up the entire Bank Act in order to deal with that particular clause? If it is found later after investigation that there is something in the Bank Act that should not be there or which brought about this trouble in connection with the Merchants Bank, we can easily amend the clause in the act. But to hold up the charters of the seventeen banks of Canada, to interfere with the stability of our financial institutions because of some alleged trouble which arose in connection with the Merchants Bank, is what I would call, if I were not in this House, silly.
Then, the hon. gentleman speaks about the "speedy changes" which are taking place.
259J
He says we cannot keep up with the industrial and economic changes which are going on; therefore we should put over the consideration of the Bank Act until next year. Well, will the changes then be any slower? Shall we slow up next year? I do not think we will; but so far as I can see, the speedy changes which are taking place now have no relation at all to the revision of the Bank Act. The Bank Act is the creature of the parliament of Canada, and we can change it whenever we like. We can come here next year, and, by the introduction of a proper measure, completely change the Bank Act, if we find it is not right. But why should we be tied down to passing the law, say next year, which is going to do for the next ten years? The hon. gentleman does not seem to understand; he does not seem to realize that this Bank Act can be changed whenever we wish to change it, and to my mind it is nonsensical for him to talk about its being rigid for the next ten years. This kind of talk may have some effect in the back concessions when my hon. friend appeals to the electors at the proper time, but he cannot make it go down with the hon. members of this House.
Then the hon. gentleman gives a third reason, something which my poor mind refuses to receive. Perhaps it is because it is late in the evening; at any rate, I fail to understand what he means. He says the Bank Act as it exists now is not affected by the weight of evidence which was adduced before the committee. I do not understand that. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would enlighten us before the House adjourns, because I should like to have it go forth that all arguments which the hon. gentleman adduced this evening amounted to nothing. I have already referred to two of them, these, I hope, have been successfully answered; as to the third, I wait for further information from the hon. gentleman.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on this all-important subject I wish to say that I intend to support the amendment placed before this committee by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman). To begin with, I would like to take the committee back to what occurred during the last three months in the Banking and Commerce committee. We held very regular sessions, and it occurred to me that any stranger going to that committee might wonder who were the members of parliament and who were the visitors, because it was usually the case that for some time after the hour was called we had as many visitors as we had

Bank Act
members. I say one might wonder who comprised this visiting class. But as we sat in that committee week in and week out we gradually got to know the faces; we realized that they represented people interested in finance. They were representatives of interested banks; they were legal advisers of the bankers-and those legal advisers were not there, I might say, for the benefit of their health. It looked strange to me that when the banking institutions of this country were on their trial, as it were, they should have so much legal support working steadily in the committee.
I suggest to the hon. gentleman that perhaps they were there to explain to some members of the committee, including the hon. gentleman himself, something about the Bank Act.
It is a pity the hon. member himself was not there.

Unfortunately we did not hear very much from the gentlemen I speak of. They reminded me very much of picture shows; you see the movements of the actors, but you do not hear their voices. They passed from member to member; those who were supporting them gave their vote, conscientiously, perhaps, but always on the one side; and that I think, was the reason why those gentlemen who, as I say, were not there for the good of their health, were in their places in the committee day in and day out. I had heard something about an hon. member of this House being called the gramaphone of Mackenzie and Mann, but I never realized the real meaning of that term until I went into the Banking and Commerce committee. Then I realized it in all seriousness, for if there ever was a gramaphone or a continuous hum of gramaphones it was those that played for the Canadian Bankers' Association.

I do not think the hon. member should be allowed to make a remark of that kind with impunity; I think he owes it to the committee to withdraw it. It might very well be retorted of my hon. friend that he is the gramaphone of the United Farmers of Alberta, who directly say to their federal representatives that they must obey the directions of that organization and that they have no right to voice their own opinions in parliament. I might make that statement with truth concerning every hon. gentleman from that province, and they would not be in a position to deny it. I say, Mr. 
Chairman, that my hon. friend has no right to make the insinuation which he does against members of parliament.

I submit that I am on perfectly safe ground. I do not mind the hon. senior member for Halifax calling me the gramaphone of certain interests that I was trying to defend in the Banking committee. I think it is a perfectly proper appellation to give anyone who is supporting a particular cause.
I said the hon. member had no right to take one side or the other; he has to do just what he is told, or be recalled.

The hon. member for Halifax will appreciate the fact that more independent spirit was shown by those members who come from that part of Canada from which I have the honour to come, than by those who come from any other section.
You admit it.

There were many tunes, but one song seemed to be continuously played, and that song was: "Why, the system is perfect, so leave it alone." That was the song always sung to us when we tried to make amendments.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would direct the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that what took place in the committee and the inability of some members to make amendments is not relevant to the particular amendment before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be pleased to bow to your decision. Perhaps I shall be in order if I refer for a momenc to the case of the Merchants Bank, and present that as a reason why we should not now give the banks a charter for ten years. Here is one of the largest banks in Canada which, with very short notice indeed and under very suspicious circumstances, goes to the wall. Some of the largest papers, some of the best known dailies of Canada, demand a full investigation, but no investigation is allowed. We have Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor as a witness before the Banking and Commerce committee, but he is particularly silent in regard to that collapse.
Was he asked any question about it?

I will refer the hon .gentleman to the minutes of the Banking and Commerce committee.

Bank Act
I was present. Let my hon. friend say what questions he was asked in that respect and what his replies were.

Another gentleman who came before that committee, Sir John Aird, denied the necessity of the Merchants Bank ever losing its identity. Sir Edmund Walker, another gentlemen who came there as a witness, claimed that somebody should have been punished. But later when the question was brought up of giving the committee an opportunity to investigate the matter further, the committee saw fit to refuse to permit that investigation. That is another reason why I am in favour of this amendment, and why I believe we should not grant the charters now for ten years, but rather for one year for the time being.
Does my hon. friend propose to ask that a new clause be inserted in the Bank Act providing for an investigation into the affairs of the Merchants Bank?

No. I did not make that statement. I am going to lay something before the House which I hope will prove that the banking system as it nQW exists is not giving the required support or filling the needs of the greatest industry in this country. We all know of the vast amount of advertising this country has done in the past to try and get settlers, and settlers of a particular kind, to come to this country. When they come here one of the institutions that they have to deal with, either directly or indirectly, and they can deal with no other it they deal in money at all, is the banking institutions. I am going to bring to the notice of this House a particular case of some people who were brought to this country some thirteen years ago, and who although starting then with the very best of chances have to-day through the actions of our present banking institutions not only gone to the wall, but are willing to get out as soon as they can. I am sure the committee will be interested in hearing read a letter of introduction that I have in my hand from Lord Strathcona. It is written to Mr. J. W. Dafoe, Manitoba Free Press, Winnipeg, Canada. It is sent from 17 Victoria Street, London S. W.

What is the date of the
letter?
The 7th of November, 1910.
Is that the original?
Did you find it in the Archives?

Hon. gentlemen will probably be sorry I did find it by the time I get through. This letter was sent to Mr. Dafoe recommending Mr. T. Hicks who was coming to this country, and this is what Lord Strathcona said:
This letter will be presented to you by Mr. T. Hicks who sails by the S.S. "Montcalm" on the 9th instant to join two of his sons who are already settled at Sedgwick, Alberta.
Sir Walter Gilbey, Bart., at whose request I furnish this introduction, informs me that Mr. Hicks will prove an acquisition; that he is not only a practical farmer, but an exceptional judge of all stock, and very many thousands of all kinds of stock have been bred and sold by him.
I commend Mr. Hicks to your consideration, and am sure he will much appreciate any advice and assistance you can kindly accord him.
Believe me,
Your very truly,
Strathcona.
Mr. Hicks came over to this country with his wife, one daughter and seven sons.
Have you found anything strange about that letter?

I will show you the results of it. Mr. Hicks, as you will recognize from this letter of Lord Strathcona, was one of the very best type of settlers that we could possibly get into this country. He came here with his seven sons and started up. He was doing very well, but now I want to read a letter from the reeve of a municipality in the vicinity of Mr. Hicks' place showing what his condition is to-day. He says:
Please find enclosed letter from Mr. Hicks who is residing close to Provost-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member to come within the rule of relevancy. If he wishes to read the letter of some eminent banker and apply it in his argument on this section that will be in order, but certainly not a letter of introduction.

This is not a letter of introduction, but a letter from the reeve of a municipality which shows what is happening to the people of this country through the action of the banks, and this man believes that the charters should not be extended for more than one year. He says:
This is one of the worst cases I have come across, although these last few days I have found several similar but on a smaller scale.
This man Hicks came in with money and established himself on land suitable only for raising stock. By the enclosed letter you will see what the banks have done to him. He happened to be one of the few who had property that the creditors could sacrifice. The debate on the immigration policy showed the government the state that this country is in. I do not need to dwell on that except to say that the people are leaving this district in hundreds, and the
Bank Act

chief thing that is driving them out is the debt and the banks holding a chattel mortgage on everything
they possess.
If your committee do not persuade the government to take control of credit out of the hands of private individuals who are using it for their own profit instead of for the good of the country, I tremble for the future of this country. People are freely talking of resistance to these inhuman methods of collecting debt.
I would earnestly suggest that your committee make an investigation into this particular case in the interests of this ruined man and also the balance of the farmers who will be in the same position when there is enough value in the amount of stock they have to make them worth selling.
Yours truly,
Thos. Pat ridge,
Reeve M. D. of Stewart.
Is he a banker?

He would make a very good banker. This is the letter he refers to. This is from Hicks. He says:
In August 1921,-

I rise to a point of order. I call your attention, Mr. Chairman, to rule 16 and the decision given under number 202 in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the House and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the House.
If we are going to hear letters written fifteen years ago by people in England commenting on the Bank Act I do not know where this debate will end.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not understand the letter is reflecting on the proceedings in this House or denying anything said by an hon. member. I would say that the hon. member has not proceeded sufficiently far for me to give a ruling on his intention.
I will read this letter. It is from Mr. Hicks, the man referred to. This letter, I may say, is dated April 23rd.
Not April 1st.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that it is doubtful whether a long recital of some difficulties a farmer had with an individual bank manager has any relevancy to the general principle of whether the bank charters should be extended for one year or ten years.
To meet your wishes I will-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am not giving a ruling at present. I am just suggesting to

the hon. member that there is doubt in my
mind as to whether the matter he is reading is relevant to the question.
I should like to read the following letter-
The letter does not appear to be accompanied by an affidavit.

I may say, Mr. Chairman, that the letter is signed and furthermore to satisfy hon. members opposite I may say here is another letter from the same man received a few days ago. He says:
I would like the case made public. Don't put initials down or say a man in the West, but tell exact my name and address, besides the bank causing mi- to lose $3,000 in actual cash.
I hope that will satisfy my hon. friend.
Is it the Merchants Bank he had dealings with?
Is the hon. member always so easily satisfied with the insolvent's own account of how he came to go to the wall?

I did not quite catch my hon. friend's question. This man was pressed absolutely unnecessarily by the bank. He had several times the amount of assets that he had liabilities with the bank, and several times they broke their promise to him. The bank saw fit to remove their manager and they have not thought fit to make good to Hicks up to the present time.

I suppose the hon. gentleman knows, as a matter of general practice that an insolvent generally gives a one-sided account of how he came to go to the wall; he generally puts the blame upon the other fellow.
I would like to say that I have had this case corroborated from five different sources and my informants are all very reliable men.
Does the hon. gentleman noi think that inasmuch as it was the Merchants Bank that was concerned, the rule "Speak nothing but good of the dead" ought to apply?

With the Merchants Bank this man had very reasonable treatment. But the Montreal Bank treated him as I have stated.
I should like to read a very short account from a local paper as follows:
District court sitting held May 17th.
This is in regard to the same bank.
A very interesting ease was decided at the sitting of the district court which was held in Provost last
Thursday before His Honor Judge Lees. The case was at the suit of Lambert Haan against the Bank of Montreal.
Haan alleged that the Provost manager of the defendant bank had agreed to pay his thresh bill on some 1,400 bushels of wheat which the bank had received. The bank denied making the agreement and claimed that for various reasons Haan's threshing lien was invalid. The court, however; held both that the agreement had been made and that Haan's threshing lien was in order and gave Haan judgment against the bank for the amount of his claim and costs.
Was there any appeal?

No appeal that I know of.
I wish to draw the attention of the committee to another case to show what satisfaction, what service, the people of that particular province are getting from the banks at the present time. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) stated this evening that the farmers of western Canada had borrowed too liberally. Would it not be just as fair to say that the banks in western Canada had lent too liberally, and that the fault on the part of the farmers is only equal to the fault on the part of the banks?

Will my hon. friend allow me to suggest that he cannot prove or disprove everything by citing individual instances of what, perhaps, are real hardships suffered by a borrower on the part of a bank. We might admit that the case to which my hon. friend referred just a moment ago was one in which the borrower, perhaps, did not receive fair treatment.
That was admitted.

Yes, and the bank manager was suspended. Might the same thing not happen in any country in the world and under any banking system? Does my hon. friend think he is contributing anything to the debate by referring to instances of this kind?

I am very glad the hon.
member for Halifax has brought this point to my notice, because in a very few minutes I am going to bring confirmation from many other sources along the same lines.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am going to tell the hon. member that it is not relevant to the particular subject matter under discussion for him to do that. There is a definite resolution before the committee, and the debate has gone rather beyond that this evening. The question is whether the bank charters shall be renewed for ten years or for one year. Reasons may be given why they should not be, but individual instances of failures, of loans,
Bank Act

of insolvencies, cannot possibly be a reason why there should not be- a renewal of the charters for either ten years or one year.

I will try to keep- within your ruling. I am in favour of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) because of the notice I have in my hand, which, in my opinion, proves that there is something radically wrong with our financial system in that it has allowed the country to get into the state in which it is at present. I am reading now a few lines from the Alberta Gazette, part 2, dated Edmonton, Tuesday, May 25, 1923. It is headed:
Notice under the Tax Recovery Act, Department of Municipal Affairs, Province of Alberta.
Notice is hereby given that proceedings have been begun under the Tax Recovery Act, 1922, against the following lands in the improvement districts in the South Alberta land registration district, and unless the lands named herein are redeemed before the 14th day-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
How can the hon.
member contend that this tax notice is relevant to the particular amendment that has been moved?

If you will allow me
half a minute-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should like to have a reason because, in my opinion, it is clearly irrelevant.

The very fact that there are advertised in this Gazette no less than 2,207,360 acres of land for sale, is proof that something is wrong, and I contend that our financial system is wrong. If our financial system is wrong, I do not see why we should give the banks a charter for ten years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member is in order in reading a tax notice.

I will come to the last matter that I will bring to the notice of the committee. We on this side of the House have made certain statements during this session in the Chamber and in the various committees, and these statements have been, at least, very much doubted, if not denied. To be sure that the statements we were making were correct, I sent out a questionnaire in regard to banking in order to find out the relationship between the banks and the people throughout a very large constituency.
I have a synopsis of this, and I am going to read it-it is short-because it is a reason why we should extend these charges for only one year at the present time. The heading of the questionnaire I sent out reads:
I wifi be very much obliged to you if you will at your earliest convenience fill in the answers below in as [The Chairman.]
accurate a manner as possible. I would ask you to make your estimates, when in doubt rather conservative than otherwise, so that I may be sure of being within the truth in any use that I may make of the information.
The first question reads:
What bank or banks are in your vicinity?
The banks included in the answers were the Bank of Montreal, the Bank of Commerce, the Royal Bank, the Union Bank, the Bank of Toronto, and the Hochelaga Bank. The second question reads:
What is the average term of farmers' notes in months ?
The answer was: Three and a half months. Imagine an industry that has a turnover usually only once in twelve months, having to renew its obligations every three and a half months! The third question reads:
Do you consider this a long enough term?
One hundred per cent said. No, decidedly not. The fourth question reads:
What is the average interest charged?
Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor, chairman of the Bankers' Association, when giving evidence before the Banking and Commerce committee, stated at first that he thought the average throughout western Canada was 7 per cent, and later he raised that to 7 or 8. In this instance, if we strike an average, the rate comes between 8 and 9 per cent. I want to give the committee just the facts. The fifth question reads:
Does the bank charge what is usually known as bankers' discount, that is, deduct interest from a note prior to money being given to borrower?
Eighty-eight per cent of the answers were: Yes; twelve per cent were: No. The sixth question reads:
About what month are notes dated to become due?
The answers were that notes are renewed every few months, but they are forced to meet their notes in the fall, very often at the expense of having to sell their products on a falling market. The seventh question reads:
Is this beneficial to agriculture?
As the committee will understand, the answer was one hundred per cent: No. The eighth question reads:
Have many caveats been issued against grain which prevented the farmer from getting his money at the elevator ?
Twenty per cent of them say: Yes; eighty per cent say: No. I might say that in one of the answers that was "yes," they said "Yes, over one hundred caveats were issued at the local elevator." The ninth question reads:
Did the farmers borrow heavily to buy feed for the cattle during the winter of 1919-20?

Bank Act
Or otherwise the hard winter. Ninety-two per cent said that they did, and only eight per cent said that they did not. The tenth question reads:
Did the banks in the spring of 1920 encourage farmers to buy stock, because in their opinion they would rise in value?
Eighty-four per cent answered yes, and sixteen per cent answered no. The eleventh question reads:
Did your bank try to force farmers at a later date to sell cattle bought on their advice, even if said stock had to be sold at a loss?
Seventy-six per cent answered yes, eight per cent answered no, and sixteen per cent did not send a return. The twelfth question is:
Was this a general practice?
Fifty-six per cent answered yes, sixteen per cent answered no, twelve per cent answered some, and sixteen did not answer. The thirteenth question reads:
What percentage of satisfaction is the bank giving to your district?
This is rather interesting to the committee. Fifty-two per cent answered "Not very good." Thirty-two per cent say "None at all." Twelve per cent say they are getting some service, and four per cent send no reply.
What class of people gave those answers?
The class of people such as Lord Strathcona-	[DOT]
He is dead now. What class of people made those answers? Lord Strathcona is in heaven.
Men qualified to run a business.
What class of people made those answers?
The clients of the bank.
Were they business men or professional men?
Business farmers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to know how the hon. member can make all these questions relevant to the particular matter before the committee. I cannot see the relevancy. I do not like to rule the hon. member out of order.
I do not wish to go against the ruling of the Chair, but I think this is very valuable information.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is no reason why it should be introduced in this discussion. It must be relevant.
This questionnaire was sent to find out the feeling between the people and the bank, and whether they were willing that the charter should be granted for ten years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not relevant to this particular amendment.
The answers I am giving are the reasons why I am voting that the charter be extended for one year only at the present time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: These questions and answers are altogether irrelevant, with one exception perhaps.

I have a few more questions. The fourteenth question reads:
Has your bank requested payment of their clients' liabilities in full, with the promise of extension of credit?
Eighty-four per cent answered yes, and sixteen do not reply at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am going to rule that question out of order.
I am very sorry that that is the Chairman's ruling, but I will just give the House the last one.
May I speak-
Order, order.

May I speak to the point of order. I would like to submit that if the hon. member for Battle River shows, as he is attempting to show, I think, that the banks in western Canada are not giving satisfaction, that is relevant to the question of whether or not the charters should be extended one year or ten years. It seems to be absolutely relevant.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I refer to Denison's Decisions, where I find the following:
A general argument on a bill cannot be allowed on a particular clause.
Mr. Speaker rules that the question at present being whether this particular clause should pass a general argument can hardly be allowed upon the question.
I am reading from Denison, page 56. There is no question as to the rules. In committee the discussion must be relevant to the particular [DOT] question or clause or amendment under discussion, and a statement as to conditions industrially or otherwise in different
Bank Act

parts of the country have only a remote bearing on it, and not a direct bearing which would be necessary to bring it within the rules.

I submit there has been no opportunity given for debating this bill in the House. It received the second reading formally. It was referred to the committee. There was plenty of opportunity for discsus-sion in committee, but there has been no opportunity in the House. Our move this afternoon was ruled out of order. We are reduced to this position: Are we going to be ruled out of order-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman tell the committee why, if he had any fundamental objection to the measure, it was not brought forward on the second reading when the whole question could be discussed?

I think I can answer the question frankly. The Minister of Finance stated on that occasion, if my recollection is correct, that he desired the fullest possible discussion in the committee and he hoped the second reading would go through without discussion, and it went through.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The motion was that it
be referred to the committee on Banking and Commerce, and I suggested that there should be the fullest discussion there, and we had the fullest discussion in that committee.

I will not go against the ruling. I will not give the House what I consider is a lot of valuable information. I assure this House and the committee, that if they are going to shut their eyes to the conditions that exist, they will wake some day to a scene that they will be very sorry to see.

speechtext: Do not threaten us.

A member must not interrupt any member who is speaking by disorderly noises or in any other manner.

speechtext:
There is no question about the rule being a correct one.
[The Chairman. [
I think the rule I have read has the specific application at the present moment.
If I had not been interrupted I would have been through about ten minutes ago. Does the Chairman rule me out of order?	.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member can answer questions put to him if he wishes, but if he does not desire to answer questions he need not do so.
If I may be allowed to pursue that, there has been a continual fire of questions-
Order, order.

I draw the Chairman's attention to the fact that throughout the speech of the hon. gentleman there has been an uninterrupted fire of questions and inarticulate comments, which I think altogether unjustified, in view of the rules I have read to the House just now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would ask hon. members to permit the hon. gentleman who is speaking to continue without interruption.
You do not rule me out of order in regard to this information I am trying to give?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On the questions and answers, yes.

All right, I will abide by your ruling. I just want to say that the=e questionnaires and answers disclose conditions in the country from which we come tha t no member of the House can afford to ignore. I wish to tell the House-and this is relevant to the point at issue-that with the enormous sums of money that this country is spending year in and year out in trying to bring people to this country, that questionnaires prove that we are losing people in vast numbers, and that the few that are returning are simply lenting. I would remind hon. members that these replies show a mortgage indebtedness m the county that most of them would refuse to credit. It is because the people there have not got the sympathetic ear of the financial institutions which enjoy a monopoly, that they are crying out for relief. And when we, their representatives, put the case fairly and squarely before this House what reception do we get? We simply get ruled out of order, ridiculed, laughed at-anything but sympathy. But we are not looking for sympathy, we are looking for justice. One of the things that we are asking in justice to

Bank Act
our people is that these bank charters should be renewed for one year only, to give us an opportunity of reviewing the vast amount of evidence that has been placed before the committee.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has stated that hon. gentlemen who were putting forward amendments before the Banking and Commerce committee, were advancing something that was not of very great value. He may not have thought our suggestions were of very great value, but the hon. members who sponsored them thought they were, and put a great deal of time on their preparation. I would point out that one of the reasons why we should have these charters extended for one year only for the time being, is because of the fact that the greater percentage of the arguments we put forward in favour of our amendments were ignored, and the amendments were turned down by a silent vote. As an instance, take section 91 in regard to interest. Masses of evidence were adduced why, if we are to have a clause regulating the rate of interest, there should be a penalty for any attempt to exact anything in excess of the stipulated rate. Very few spoke against the proposal, I think only two members, yet when it came to a vote, however convincing the arguments put forward might have been, they failed t; influence the committee, and the amendment was defeated by the silent vote which never failed to function on such occasions.
It showed their good sense.

It may have, but it showed that they had not the good sense to speak to the question. The hon. member for Halifax also stated-and I was very sorry to hear him, because personally I have a very great regard for him-that foolish and dangerous ideas had been put forward. I cannot understand why he should make that statement in view of the fact that so few of these so-called foolish and dangerous ideas were considered. At any rate, if that was his opinion as the chairman of the committee, it was natural that he would not be in favour of them. He asserted that ample and due consideration was given to all amendments. I am sorry to say that I cannot agree with him In the last few days some very important amendments were put forward, in some cases without the slightest criticism being offered against them, indeed, with several members of the committee speaking in their favour, but those amendments were solidly turned down by the silent vote.
It is for these reasons, and for many others that I could mention if I cared to take up any more time of the committee, that I am in favour of, and intend to vote for, this amendment that the charters be extended for one year only.

It was not my intention to say anything on this subject to-night, but it seems to me that a change of programme would be acceptable to the House. Now, I have been thirty-one years in this country and have been doing business with the banks off and on during that time, and I have always found them ready to do what was right. I have always got money when I wanted it, and at a fair rate of interest; and when I had any money to deposit I always got a fair rate of interest. The fault with most people at the present time is that they want to start in at llie top of the ladder. They do not want to do as men did thirty years ago,-work to get a start. The fault of many people is that they borrow all the money they can get, and instead of repaying it when they sell their crop they will go and buy an auto and run around the country. I state the facts of the case.
As I have already said, I have no fault to And with the banking system, and I think it is up to the House to give an extension of the bank charters for ten years in order to create business stability in the country. If we begin extending the charters from year to year, what confidence will any person have in the country? It is going to do harm, and, I repeat, I think it is up to the House to extend the charters for another ten years. If a certain class of people want loans there are other means of securing them.
They have not got any security to give.

If they have the security they can get all the loans they want without any trouble. I have always found that if you do the right thing with the banks, the banks will do the right thing with you. If I have any fault to find with the banks at all it is that they are too free with their money. 1 believe that the curse of this country today is too much borrowing and not enough production. If people would only work for what they want it would be better for the Dominion as a whole.
Mr. Chairman, as there are a number of other members who wish to speak to the question, I would suggest that it might be advisable to adjourn the debate.

Go ahead.
Bank Act

I am prepared to go ahead, Mr. Chairman. It seems to me that the amendment is very reasonable indeed. We are accepting the revision so far as it has been accomplished up to date, and we are simply asking that the charters be granted for one year, so that between now and next session we may have an opportunity to study the mass of evidence dealing with the whole question of our financial and banking system. It seems to me that the government would be well advised to consent to such a fair and moderate suggestion.
I had intended to speak at some length, but there will be other opportunities for dealing with certain phases of the subject that I wish to take up, and therefore I will content myself for the present by simply pointing out very briefly the situation that faces us to-day. There is no doubt that Canada, along with many other nations, is in a very serious condition. This is doubtless partly due to the war-how much it is hard to say; but whether it is due to one cause or another the condition is admittedly serious. Now, in the face of that condition; in face of the fact that a very large volume of evidence has been submitted to the committee; in face of the fact that a number of other amendments have been suggested to the bill by members of the committee; in face of the fact that a number of further investigations, such as that into the Merchants Bank fiasco, have been demanded by members of the committee, the government apparently propose to wash their hands of the whole affair; to clean up, so to speak, and enact legislation for another ten years. I submit that that is a very dangerous procedure. It has been admitted by a good many members cf the committee on all sides after hearing the evidence that, possibly, very fundamental changes in our financial system will be necessary during the next ten years. If that is so, surely we would be well advised if we simply granted the charters for one year, meanwhile looking into the evidence so that next year we shall be in a position to decide what should be done.
I want to make one or two remarks on the Merchants Bank case. There has been a good deal of confusion of mind regarding the motion that was moved in the Banking and Commerce committee some time ago respecting this matter. The purpose of the proposed investigation is not to again try Mr. Macarow and the others. They were indicted on a certain specific charge; they were tried, and they were acquitted. So far as the wrongdoing is concerned, nobody knows who is to blame. Evidently there was some falsification of returns. We have a situation which I think

is almost without a parallel. The trial has come off, somebody must have been guilty, but we do not know who. The purpose of the proposed investigation is not to try these men over again but to get from men who know the inside of this affair information that is highly necessary if the various clauses of the Bank Act, especially those having to do with inspection, returns, and so on, are to be properly drafted so that the future may be safeguarded. I submit that the calling of Mr. Macarow, the general manager of the Merchants Bank, would be entirely in order, entirely proper; and the turning down of that suggestion in the committee created in my mind grave suspicions as to what lay behind the action, particularly in view of rumours that have been circulated regarding the affair. I do not know what truth there was in these rumours, but in view of the circumstances; in view of the mystery surrounding a number of these matters, it was entirely in order that these men should come here and give any information that members of the House should think fit to ask them to furnish.
What are your suspicions?
I do not propose to be led into that to-night.
Because you have not any.
I have.
Why not tell us what they are?

They have already been referred to in the discussion. I am not going to deal at length with the Merchants Bank case to-night.
Further there is great need in Canada for some rural credit legislation. We do not know at present how far this may be worked out independently of our present banking system or how far it may be necessary to link it up with the latter. Therefore, until we have something more definite, more concrete, more specific with regard to the whole question of rural credits, in my opinion it would be the wisest thing to give a temporary extension of the charters of the Canadian banks, and then if any changes are desirable between now and next year when we have the report of the committee on rural credits and when the matter can be gone into to some extent, we shall be in a very much better position to decide what should be done. There is no doubt that this is a matter that needs immediate attention; it has been admitted in the committee by men on all sides that that is the case. It is therefore, a very fair proposal indeed that until this matter takes shape we

Bank Act
should not give any very considerable extension to the bank charters under the present terms.
In addition to that there has been submitted to the committee, but hardly discussed at all, the question of a federal reserve bank. This is a most important question not only as it relates to our present banking system, but also as it may be linked up with the whole question of rural credits and smaller banks. We shall have to give it some consideration. I am inclined to think from what little information I have on the question that it is almost a necessary part of a rural credit system. This thing is as yet undiscussed, uninvestigated by the committee.
I submit also that the whole question of cooperative banking, which has been so successful elsewhere, is something we ought to consider before our financial system is crystallized in its present shape for another ten years.
We heard something in the committee also about the Australian Commonwealth Bank, a government bank in Australia which seems to have given a great deal of satisfaction. This, too, in its possible application to the Canadian financial system has not received any consideration; it has been mentioned once or twice, but we have not had time to look into the matter.
There is another matter which in my judgment is one of prime importance, concerning which I had intended to speak at some length. I shall only refer to it now; I will leave the discussion of the stabilizing of the purchasing power of money until we reach the clause on interest, where I think it may appropriately be brought up again. But this is one of the most vital questions in the entire field of economics. The whole world has suffered tremendously in recent years from fluctuations in the purchasing power of money. Professor Irving Fisher, of Yale University, who has evolved a plan for the stabilizing of the purchasing power of money, gave evidence before the committee. But it has not been discussed by the committee, although it is very closely linked up with our whole banking system, so far as the control of interest rates is in some degree a means of stabilizing prices. Moreover it has already been stated that a number of representative bodies throughout Canada have asked that the charters be extended for just one year so that time may be afforded for examination of the evidence which has been submitted. As the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) said not very long ago, there are a great many members of this House who have not been privileged to attend the meet-[Mr. Good.)
ings and follow the evidence, who have not had time yet even to read it, and who, I think, should not be called upon to express themselves in a vote at the present time in any final way. I think they would appreciate very much the opportunity which a year's extension of the bank charters would give them to look into this evidence which has been placed on record. In that connection, Mr. Chairman, I want to say something that is not very pleasant to say, but I think perhaps it is necessary. I have seen some things this year that I never thought I would see in a Canadian parliament and I must say that my faith in the sincerity and integrity of people who have the control of policy has been somewhat shattered by what I 'have seen this year. I do not like to make a statement like that, but I think perhaps I had better.
If the reflection is intended for a member of the House, the hon. member's remark is certainly out of order.
I will say no more, Mr. Chairman.
Speak for yourself.
What does the hon. member mean? Why talk in this cryptic way? Have we got integrity in this House or in the committee or have we not?

I think the hon. member on consideration will admit that applying such a term to gentlemen who are in control of policy in this House is certainly unparliamentary. The expression had better be withdrawn.
I will explain myself, Mr. Chairman, if hon. gentlemen wish me to.
Go ahead. Do not talk in innuendoes all the time.
Explain.
I want to mention one matter, Mr. Chairman-
You could not back up your statement.
Withdraw.
If necessary I can read the hon. member the rule of the House. I think that his words should be withdrawn.

Then I will withdraw at your request, Mr. Chairman. During the hearings of the committee we learned just about enough from the accountant, Mr. Edwards, who made some partial investigation into the Merchants
Bank Act

Bank affair, to make it very necessary indeed to carry out a fuller investigation. I would like to recall the evidence he submitted in connection with his partial investigation. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) said during the course of his remarks that bank failures cannot be prevented by legislation. Now I want very respectfully to call that statement in question. What is the purpose of the efforts that we have made this year on the committee to stop some of the loopholes, to remedy some of the defects, if it is not to make more difficult such failures as have taken place in the past?
I said that.
I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member left a very different impression on some members of the committee. He did on my mind1 at all events.

I said it was our duty to strengthen our legislation so as to make failures as difficult as possible to occur, but I did express the view that I did not think legislation would make absolutely impossible bank failures or any other kind of failures.

I am very glad to have this explanation from the hon. member because I think now he and I agree absolutely in regard to this matter. The purpose of our legislation is to make these things more difficult to occur. Of course, everybody admits that you cannot remedy the defects or frailties of human nature altogether by legislation, but I submit, Mr. Chairman, that legislation can do a great deal in many directions for assisting in that particular way.
The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) wanted to know what the Merchants Bank affair had to do with this Bank Act. I would like to reply to that question in this way: If we do not know, as we do not at the present time, what lay behind that situation we cannot take the necessary precautions except in so far as we may apply general rules to provide safeguards-

May I ask the hon. member a question? I have never been a supporter of Canada's banking system, but I would ask the hon. member for Brant this question. I understand he is one of the directors and vice-president of the United Farmers of Ontario Co-operative stores. Would he mind reading to the committee a report of the meeting at Toronto last fall of the shareholders of the United Farmers Cooperative stores, which have been far from a success to their shareholders, and tell the committee why he did not apply the advice he 
is giving now in the administration of these stores? We had a Farmers Bank in Toronto in which 2,690 widows and orphans lost their all. The bank was run on theory and such lines as the hon. gentleman talks of. Will he please read to the committee the press report on the row at the United Farmers of Ontario Co-operative stores meeting last fall and the result of the failure of the Farmers Bank?
May I ask the hon. member if he will kindly answer the question I put to him: Why does he not apply the same principle he is advocating here to the United Farmers of Ontario Co-operative stores?

Mr. Chairman, very much of what I desire to say had I been able to speak earlier in the evening has already been said, but I wish to join my voice with those who are protesting against the jamming through of this bill for ten years at the present session. I share the opinion of hon. members in this quarter of the Chamber who have held that a proper investigation must be made into the Merchants Bank case before the House, or a committee of the House, is competent to deal with the Bank Act in a manner that the public of this country desire as the result of the fiasco that has been witnessed. No due consideration has been given to the mass of evidence adduced before the committee. That point has also been raised by hon. members sitting round me and I share the opinion of those who have made known their views upon it.
There was a refusal during the last few daj's of the sittings of the committee on Banking and Commerce to investigate or to discuss the Federal Reserve system of the United States. I should like to call the attention of this House to the answer of the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) when this question came up. He said: "It is not worth calling witnesses half a mile, that all the evidence, all the stuff that was required, could be secured in the library." What an extraordinary statement to be made by an opponent of an investigation into the Federal Reserve system of the United States, one of the greatest and one of the most famous systems in the world, "that you could find all the information about it in the library". Why did we go into committee to deal with this matter if you could find all about it in the library? Why discuss anything if you could find all about it in the library. That is one of the chief arguments of those who seem to be particularly interested in passing the Bank Act this session. Now, the refusal to investigate the Merchants Bank case by that committee-
Order.

-has been in my opinion one of the most disastrous things the Liberal party has ever perpetrated in this country, and it will react to the
Bank Act

discredit of the Liberal party everlastingly. There will be protests by the people of this country in a short time that will astonish hon. members sitting opposite. They, perhaps, cannot yet conceive the immense feeling that is already gaining ground in connection with the matter.
Where is it?

May I read from the Montreal Star of April 28, 1923, an expression of opinion on the subject:
The sudden wreckage of the Merchants Bank shocked the people of Canada. Even yet they do not fully understand what happened. They are not convinced that, it was necessary to cUose the doors on an ancient and honourable institution and have its assets turned over to a rival. It is true that the shareholders suffered most and that there is no more reason to protect holders of bank shares than those who invest in other enterprises, but the whole banking system was put under suspicion by a collapse and an absorption for causes which are still imperfectly understood and as to which no explanation has been offered which has seemed to be adequate.
On this ground of lack of information alone, an investigation of the Merchants Bank case, in conjunction with the whole discussion of the Bank Act, should have been taken by the committee on Banking and Commerce.
May I be permitted to ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Does my hon. friend believe in the Montreal Star?

May I suggest to the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier most quietly and respectfully that the very ethics of his profession ought to have been sufficient to have prevented him from interrupting me when I was discussing the Merchants Bank case, seeing that the hon. member, I understand, was attorney for one of the parties in the case.
I do not take lessons in ethics from the hon. member for Bow-legged River, or whatever his constituency is.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman has just made a reference to the constituency of my hon. friend (Mr. Garland), which should be withdrawn.
I did not understand the hon. member to reflect on Mr. Garland's integrity.
I ask my hon. friend from Medicine Hat not to deal too drastically with the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier, but rather to sympathize with him.
Take your medicine.

In regard to the investigation into the Merchants Bank fiasco another question arose-apart altogether from that appalling collapse itself- in the minds of the public, and that was the question of mergers. But before I pass on to that I would like to quote, as another reason why the bank charters should not be renewed for ten years at the present session, a statement from the Canadian Annual Review, 1921. The quotation, I can assure hon. members will not be lengthy. I have no more desire than they have to prolong this discussion, but I do desire to put myself on record on this important question. At page 40 of the Canadian Annual Review of 1921, after a lengthy and very clearly defined statement of the history and standing of the Merchants Bank, the following is written:
On December, 16 Montreal heard with astonishment and the country with absolute amazement that the chairman of fhe Montreal Stock Exchange had received from Sir Montague Allan, president of the bank, the following letter:
"You are requested herewith to withdraw Merchants Bank of Canada stock from your list as arrangements have been made with the Bank of Montreal, subject to the approval of the Governor in Council 'and the shareholders of both banks, to take over the Merchants Bank."
I rise to a point of order. Is it relevant for the hon. member to read this matter before the committee?	.

I do not
think so, for this reason:	In the discussion
of clause 5 and the amendment thereto, I frankly confess that I cannot see how any aspect of banking or the banking system cannot be made relevant to the question. It is true that on other questions some of these matters would be utterly out of order. For instance, on the interest clause, you could discuss interest ad lib., its effect on the people and conditions arising out of it; but on this particular clause which refers to the extension of the charters for a term of ten years, if I happened to be in the chair-and I am glad I am not-I would find it difficult to rule against any discussion of the banking system of Canada.
Amongst other matters that I would like to call to the attention of this committee-and as an indication of my goodwill in this matter, I will lay aside any further quotations concerning the Almanac and the Merchants Bank -is that one of the most astonishing things to the people of this country is that at that time the Merchants Bank stock was worth $157. There is involved in this question, as I said, a moment ago, the question of mergers. The people of Canada are becoming more and more satisfied that the development of a money oligarchy in this country is not in the best interest of Canada. The development of that oligarchy has gone on under this Bank Act. No provision has yet been made in the Bank Act to prevent that. There are no restrictions on mergers; everything in that connection is left to the Minister of Finance. We find that in 1904 there were thirty-four banks in Canada with about 1,100 branches. In 1920, there were only eighteen banks, and to-day there are only seventeen with fully six or seven thousand branches. These banks were absorbed, swallowed up in the most extraordinary fashion. A few failed, but most of them were absorbed by larger banks. There seems to have been a contest between the Bank of Montreal and the Royal Bank of Toronto to see which would absorb or grab up the largest number. I am quoting from a book written by Mr. Baker, called "Money Monopoly vs. The Community Dollar" at page 84:
It will be remembered that in an earlier chapter it was stated that in 1904 bank capital was equivalent to 11 per cent of total assets, while in 1920 the ratio
had been decreased to 4 per cent. Therefore, not only did the banks fail to maintain their position in this respect, but they carried on a policy of expansion until they had four times as. many branches with only a ratio of 4 per cent between capital and total assets.
This is but one of the evils that follow m the train of mergers. That question has not been properly or duly considered. Leaving aside this matter of the discussion of the investigation of the Merchants Bank, and that is one of the reasons why this amendment should carry, I should like to ask the following questions in the hope that some hon. member opposite will answer them. This would, perhaps, clear the minds of hon. members in this part of the chamber on this matter and not make them so convinced that the rights of the Canadian people are in jeopardy as their present position would indicate:
Is it a fact that the directors of the Merchants Bank were compelled to sell out for protection of creditors or shareholders? Or were there other considerations which played a part in the impelling process ?
These are questions I should like to have answered, possibly by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) or by the Minister of Finance when he speaks:
Did the Bank of Montreal pay any more for the Merchants Bank than it was worth? If it did should the public not know how it covered up its loss? If it did not, and it is not likely that the Bank of Montreal did so, how is it that a corporation with capital intact and a surplus of 15 per cent of its capital, could be impelled to sell out to protect its shareholders and depositors? Since when have corporations become insolvent because they could pay their creditors, pay their stockholders, and distribute a dividend from surplus of 15 per cent? If the institution was strained for ready cash to meet its clearing obligations, why could it not have borrowed from the government just as other banks do when they are strained? Why did not the Bank of Montreal and other banks assist the Merchants Bank if its stock was worth 115?
In fact, it was worth more than that at one time, just prior to the merger:
Is it possible that the associated banks did not like the business methods of the Merchants Bank, such as founding and advertising Christmas clubs?
There are many other questions, but I will leave these with the hon. members, and if they can answer them they can satisfy me more than I expect to be satisfied by the members of this committee.
Perhaps the greatest reason that can be put forward for the extension of these charges for one year only at this time is that we have in this country admittedly, admitted by the greatest bankers that those who are interested could get before the committee on banking, a gap in the credit structure of Canada, a gap for which no provision is made and for which they say no provision can be made under the banking system. Yet no one of those bankers came to us, nor did the Bankers' Association



Bank Act
come to us with any proposal designed to cover the gap. As we have no suggestion offered in this regard, to whom shall we go? Hon. members opposite have suggested a rural credit scheme. All rural credit schemes in Canada to-day are based in the final analysis on the banks, and yet we know that the banks are antagonistic to rural schemes. They have shown that only too clearly in Manitoba and Ontario. Hon. members opposite say: Be calm; be quiet; we will get a rural credit scheme for you some time, we do not know just when, but some time. I ask: What are you going to do? There is no proposal in this regard before the committee. There is no justification for the statements they are making. If they have a rural credit scheme, we would be delighted to consider and discuss it.
There are in this country three great papers, in particular the Financial Post, the Montreal Star, the Winnipeg Free Press, and indeed many others that have asked that these bank charters be extended for only one year at this time. You have heard hon. members around me speak of organizations that have asked for the same thing. Mention was made by the hon. member for Victoria, Alta. (Mr. Lucas), to the effect that Mr. Tom Moore had sent him a letter embodying or containing resolutions from various trades and labour councils of Victoria, Calgary, Edmonton, and various other places. The senior member for Halifax interrupted him, and suggested that Mr. Moore had been before the committee but that he had not brought that question up, that it had not been discussed and he had no suggestions to offer. I would submit to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) that perhaps Mr. Moore had a few weeks in which to consider this question since he left the committee and had decided that it was in the best interests of the Canadian people, and in addition to that had secured these resolutions from the Trades and Labour Councils. May I say further, Mr. Chairman, that when the senior member for Halifax says that no good and sufficient reasons have been brought before this House for the extension of the charter for one year. I would submit that when these bodies of highly organized, and I say, highly intelligent people - labour, the farmers, the governments of Alberta and of Manitoba -have seen fit to make this request, surely that alone should be a good and sufficient reason. The people have not had time to consider the evidence. They have not had time to digest the matter properly and to come to a decision. Many proposals have been brought forward. None of them has 
received due consideration. We hope they will soon. They will have to, in my opinion some time or other.
In closing, let me emulate the example of the member for George Etienne Cartier, who is an adept at facetiousness and telling humorous stories. The hon. gentlemen likened the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine) to the cuttlefish. May I say that the hon. member himself (Mr. Jacobs) reminds me of the story of a darkey I once read about, who lived in the cornfield country of the South. In the midst of a thunderstorm this darkey was driving a team of mules home late at night. Between the flashes of lightning there was dense darkness, and he could see nothing, not even the road, he was terror-stricken, and the mules were getting more restless all the time. When the lightning flashed he would see the road for a moment or two, and it temporarily renewed his courage. After a time the poor old darkey could stand it no longer, and then he prayed as I do, " Oh, Lord, let there be less noise and more light".

I regret that the government has seen fit to compel the House to sit to this late hour for the consideration of what I think is the most important subject that will come before this parliament this session. There is no subject of any greater importance to the people of this country than the revision of the Bank Act. The matter of currency and credit is one of prime importance to the people of this country. I feel that the inquiry by the committee on Banking and Commerce into the working of the Bank Act during the past ten years was very inadequate, but so far as the inquiry was carried on, it seemed to me that it was amply proved before the committee that the banking situation in this country was very far from satisfactory. If that is the case, I cannot see why the Finance Minister is so determined that the charters must be renewed for ten years. I believe that some of our own bankers are quite concerned in regard to the situation which exists in Canada to-day; yet the Finance Minister says we must put this act through and he will brook no delay. He says: "You must do nothing which will interefere with the confidence of the public", but he has done nothing to find out whether the public confidence has been misplaced. I wonder whether he has heard any rumours to the effect that one of our banks, possibly more than one, is not in very good shape to-day. I wonder whether he is expecting that before another year passes he will have applications for the approval of one or more mergers.

Two hon. gentlemen from the Progressive party told us that the whole thing is going to the bad inside of ten years.
If one or two go each year, they might all be gone before long. I do not want to make any prediction, but those are possibly not idle rumours that we hear.
It does not do much good to talk about them.

No, it does not. I wonder what would do some good about it. It might be just as well if we knew more about it, but I may say very frankly that it did not seem to me that it was the wish of that committee that we should know anything we could be prevented from finding out. I hope that is not unfair, Mr. Chairman. I do not want to be unfair. I simply said it appeared to me that way. In this country we have seen our chartered banks decrease from 34 in 1901 to 17 in 1923. In 1911, the paid-up capital of our banks was $96,000,000. In 1923, it had increased to $135,000,000. I am giving round figures. That is a very small increase, a trifle over 25 per cent, but in the same time our deposits in the Canadian banks had increased from $926,000,000 to $1,995,000,000. That is considerably more than double. In the same time our total trade in Canada has increased from $741,000,000 to $2,450,000,000, an increase of over 300 per cent. In the same time the bank loans have increased from $986,000,000 in 1911, to $1,851,000,000 to-day. That is practically double.
