speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I draw the hon. member's attention to it. I do not say he has reached that point yet.

I want to lead up to this fact, Mr. Chairman; that the bank business of Canada is now in the hands of the directors of seventeen banks, and, through the Bankers' Association, the directors of three or four of the different banks are able to dictate the financial policy of this country.
I think, Mr. Chairman, it is quite relevant to bring that to the attention of the committee as one reason why it would be quite proper to accept the amendment offered by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man) and see if we cannot within the next year amend the Bank Act to free the country from the control of these few men. If, Mr. Chairman, I might be allowed to use the expression of Sir John Aird before the committee on Banking and Commerce in referring to certain railway corporations, I would say we are now in the hands of a banking octopus, and if we have any more mergers the hold of this octopus upon the general public will be that much stronger.
The present state of affairs is particularly unfortunate in that the directors of some of our larger banks are controlling the board of" governors of our leading universities. Quite recently I was told by a professor that he dared not criticize the Bank Act as some members of the board of governors of his university were bank directors and he might lose his job. These directors not only control our universities but also our industries, and, indeed, it might even be said that they control our government. Our peculiar banking system has made this possible, as the whole tendency is toward centralization. The savings of the people are taken from the smaller towns and rural communities to build up a few of the large cities. The funds of the hanks are used to finance schemes under the control of the directors, and very often I imagine at a lower rate of interest than can be secured by those engaged in these industries in the smaller towns and cities, making it very hard for them to compete with the larger organizations. Right in this connection. Mr. Chairman, I might be allowed to quote two or three paragraphs from an address by Mr. Andrew Jay Fame, Chairman of the Board of Waukesha National Bank, Wisconsin, at a Bankers' Association meeting in the-
Bank Act

United States in reference to our banking system. He says:
In Canada some seventeen central banks (reduced from more than thirty some years ago) now skim the cream from over 4,000 branches, leaving only the skim milk for the rural and suburban populations. Branches have no local stockholders, no presidents, or cashiers. They practically pay no taxes and have figureheads for managers, subject to alien officers' orders. The most serious objection is practically no profits are distributed locally where they are made, thus impoverishing the nation at large for the sole benefit of monopolizers in the great centres.
Statistics clearly show that failures of banks and losses to depositors in Canada, compared with our National Banking System, exceed ours several times over. These facts are confirmed by at least one exmanager of a big central bank in Canada and by other authorities I am not at Liberty to quote. Her banking power is less than little Massachusetts alone. She is asleep compared to our progress.
He then quotes from an article in the Toronto Star of some years ago on the Canadian branch banking system.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must really stop the hon. member. I do not see how this could be relevant to the question of whether the bank charters should be renewed for one year or ten years. The quotation deals with the general principle of banking.
I was using this argument, Mr. Chairman, because I thought the committee should investigate to see whether our Bank Act might not be improved in respect to this particular system.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member knows that this committee has very limited powers of investigation. The bill was referred to this committee for the purpose of discussing these sections and reporting or not reporting it. This committee has not the powers of a standing committee.

Mr. Chairman, if I might be allowed to quote one sentence from this editorial I will be satisfied. It says:
Monster "banking monopoly a leech at Canada's throat killing local industry, depopulating rural districts. Centralization of almost entire financial power in the hands of a few capitalists has resulted from our much vaunted banking system. Almost total extermination of local banks.
Planting of a "branch" to suck our local earnings, etc.
I should like to read a little more of this editorial, Mr. Chairman, but it will keep. The small percentage of the paid up capital of our banks compared to the deposits results, I think, in our banks becoming panic-stricken in times of financial stringency, and they close down on their customers when they think deflation is imminent. There is no doubt that in the past this has caused great loss to their borrowers and very often to
TMr. Coote.]
the banks themselves, I think, because the assets under forced liquidation were not sufficient to pay the debtors' liabilities. Our whole credit structure is built up on the confidence which the public have in the system-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Surely, the hon. member is dealing with the general principle of banking and the credit system. I do not see how it is possible by any stretch of the imagination to connect this with any reason why bank charters should not be granted for ten years but for one year only. It is my duty to rule the hon. gentleman out of order.

Mr. Chairman, I was just about to bring to the attention of the committee what I think is one of the main reasons for this postponement, namely, that the committee on Backing and Commerce absolutely refused to call a witness who was acquainted with the actual working of the Federal Reserve Banks in the United States. I wished to argue that the special committee should have called the witness.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Any failure of a special committee, or a lulling of its chairman, is not reviewable by this committee, and is not an argument presentable in this committee on this particular section.
I do not know what argument would be relevant if that is not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not relevant, and I have so ruled.

I do not know what better reason could be advanced, Mr. Chairman, and if that is your ruling I have very little more to say. I wished, Sir, to put before this committee the action of the special committee on Banking and Commerce with regard to one or two other matters.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This committee has no power to deal with the ruling of a special committee. If the chairman of that committee submitted the question, and it was decided in the affirmative or the negative, it cannot be reviewed by this committee.

Then I will have very little more to say, because that was my chief reason for asking for support to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer. It does seem to me that the bill as brought down is very inadequate to deal with the situation which exists in Canada to-day. The Minister of Finance, if he had been well acquainted with the situation in this country, should have done something more to meet the situation than he has done in the legislation now proposed. I have some other in-

Bank Act
formation here that I would have liked to put before the committee, particularly in regard to the Commonwealth Bank,-how it would be applicable to this country; how it would improve, I think, the banking system of this country if it were introduced here, and the benefit it might be to this government and the country at large. But owing to the narrow limits within which we are compelled to keep by your ruling, Mr. Chairman,
I do not at this time care to say anything further except that I trust this amendment will be given honest consideration by the members of the committee.

I would like again to protest against the exclusion of evidence of this sort. It does seem to me that the presentation by the hon. member for Macleod of certain matters dealing with the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, as bearing upon the question of postponements, would be entirely relevant.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have ruled that it is not relevant, and I cannot in any way see that it is relevant. The question is on the amendment.
Amendment (Mr. Speakman) negatived; Yeas, 27; Nays, 65.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 8-Particulars of Act of Incorporation.
May I ask the government if it is their intention to press on with the Bank Act all night?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. At a very early stage, as soon as we meet a clause to which an amendment is proposed, we will let it stand over and have the committee rise We might run through these uncontested clauses.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 13-First meeting of subscribers.
I intended to move an amendment to section 20 asking for permission to establish smaller banks, and it would necessitate-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We may go on until that clause is reached; then I shall be glad to move that the committee rise.

I submit that the hon. member for Macleod has not been fully heard. I think he was going on to explain when interrupted that this section if passed now would prevent the formation of smaller banks under section 20.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman desires to move an amendment to it, I will move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 1.40 &.m. (Tuesday).
Tuesday, June 19, 1923
